World.title: Tico Time and Why Life in Costa Rica Doesn’t Always Run on Schedule
World.content:
I don’t want to hear about Tico Time. Where did that expression even originate? It has been around for at least the 35 years I have lived here. It was likely coined by some impatient gringo who first said it in a voice of irritation and disgust. Personally I’ve never had a problem with a casual approach to punctuality.

If I wanted to be controlled by the clock, I’d have never left my nine to five phone company job in Washington, DC. One of the many positives of life here is the laid back, pura vida outlook that says that being late for social gatherings and other appointments is not a crime. And the reality is that even if you leave with time to spare to make a meeting, there are obstacles awaiting you as soon as you step out the door. Take what happened to me last week.

I had a doctor’s appointment in town. I left early, to allow myself time to park in a public lot and walk to the medical building. I took my usual route, only to find that the one-lane bridge by the river was closed as rains had swollen the river, which then washed away much of the earthen structure supporting each side of the bridge.

I turned around, headed back up the hill, past my house and came to a crawl behind the municipal garbage truck. Something was happening at the barrio grade school and cars were parked along both sides of the narrow street. For the next few minutes, unable to pass, I breathed the pungent air and watched the workers fling leaking bags of garbage into the grinding maw of the truck. Finally, the truck made a turn and I was able to proceed.

At the intersection to the four lane highway, traffic crawled. There had been a small crash, a fender bender, and the drivers waited outside their cars for the guy from INS to show up and write up an accident report. Five minutes later, I was passing the barely damaged cars, already late for my appointment.

These are but minor inconvenience compared to the delays that mount when extreme nature decides to make its presence felt. Landslides close important highways for days at a time. Flooding chases people to higher ground. About ten years ago, I arrived in San Jose for an outgoing flight that was cancelled because Volcan Turrialba erupted.

The runways were covered in ash and visibility was limited. Juan Santamaria airport looked like a hostel for stranded vagabonds. Hundreds of passengers stuck waiting, lounging in chairs, hunkered down on the floor. I spent the night at a hotel Alajuela and was lucky to catch a flight out the next day.

There is a week every year– the final week of July leading to the Dia de la Virgin on the second of August. Depending on where you are in the country, you may be delayed by groups of true believers, walking toward Cartago. And there was a time in Costa Rica when it was common for protesting groups to block highways, sometimes for days, to get the attention of the government, but that practice was made illegal a few years back, so that is one less delay to encounter.

As for my doctor’s appointment– I arrived fifteen minutes late– and waited another 30 minutes until the doctor could see me. Pura Vida!

World.title: Costa Rica Vehicle Thefts Hit a Ten-Year High
World.content:
If you own a car here, it is more likely to be stolen now than at any point in the past ten years. Costa Rica recorded 5,146 vehicle thefts in 2025, according to open statistics from the Organismo de Investigación Judicial (OIJ). That is the highest annual figure of the decade, up from 4,289 in 2016 — a 20% increase.

What makes the number worth paying attention to is what happened around it. Over the same ten years, almost every other property crime went the other way. Muggings, larcenies, break-ins at homes and businesses, and thefts of items from inside parked cars all trended downward.

Vehicle theft did not follow and after bottoming out at 3,217 cases in 2020, it climbed every single year from 2021 through 2025. Part of that is simple arithmetic as there are far more cars to steal than there used to be. Costa Rica finished 2025 with 2,087,356 vehicles covered by mandatory SOA insurance, 9.1% more than the 1,913,266 registered a year earlier.

But more cars on the road does not really explain why this one category rose while everything else fell. Something changed about the crime itself and the answer, according to specialists whose analysis accompanied the OIJ data, is that stealing a car stopped being a job for one or two opportunists and became a supply chain.

Organized networks now handle it in stages — one person takes the vehicle, another strips it, and intermediaries move the parts to workshops, to businesses, or directly to buyers who want a cheap replacement bumper or gearbox. That matters in order to show you how you protect yourself.

A car is no longer stolen because someone wants to drive it. It is stolen because its parts are worth more disassembled than the whole vehicle is worth intact, and because those parts are easy to sell without anyone asking where they came from. Which means the thing that keeps your car safe is not just making it hard to break into. It is making it slow to move and slow to take apart.

A steering lock, a tracker, a car that gets parked somewhere visible rather than somewhere convenient — these work because they add minutes, and the whole model depends on the vehicle disappearing fast. The OIJ statistics do not show how many of the 5,146 thefts were committed by organized structures rather than by individuals acting alone, so treat that as a pattern the investigators describe rather than a number you can verify.

Where you live changes the picture considerably. Eight of the country’s cantons finished 2025 with fewer vehicle thefts than they recorded in 2016, bucking the national trend entirely. Santa Ana posted the largest drop in raw numbers, falling from 76 cases in 2016 to 31 in 2025 — 45 fewer thefts. It also slid from 14th place to 44th out of 84 cantons ranked from most to fewest.

That decline was not a straight line. Santa Ana dipped to 29 cases in 2021, then rose again to 44 in 2022, 45 in 2023 and 66 in 2024 before dropping sharply last year. Escazú, San Rafael, Heredia, Sarapiquí and Aserrí also closed below their 2016 figures, though their paths were similarly uneven and several saw rebounds in the intervening years.

Heredia is the useful cautionary case. It went from 207 thefts in 2016 to 178 in 2025, a 14% reduction — and still finished fifth in the country, having been fourth a decade earlier. Falling numbers do not automatically mean a low-risk canton. They can just mean a slightly less bad one.

One technical note on the rankings. In 2016 Costa Rica had 81 areas; it now has 84. Position changes between the two years reflect that shift as well as actual movement in theft numbers, so a area that dropped a few places has not necessarily improved.

If your vehicle is stolen, report it to the OIJ immediately rather than waiting to see if it turns up. The parts chain moves within hours, and a report filed the same day is the only realistic window in which a vehicle gets recovered whole. Have your plate number, chassis number (VIN) and your cédula or passport ready before you call, because you will be asked for all three.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Monteverde Cloud Forest Is Drying Despite Heavy Rain
World.content:
Monteverde remains one of Costa Rica’s wettest places, receiving more than 2,500 millimeters (98 inches) of rain a year. Yet scientists are finding signs of drought in the plants that help give the famous cloud forest its name. The apparent contradiction is the focus of a new PBS science report examining changes inside Monteverde’s forest canopy.

Researchers say the problem is not simply how much rain falls each year. It is how long dry spells last and how often clouds and mist come into direct contact with the forest. In a cloud forest, water does not arrive only as rain. Low clouds move through the trees, leaving moisture on leaves, branches, mosses, ferns and orchids. This process, sometimes called horizontal rain, keeps the canopy wet and slowly releases water into the soil and streams below.

But as temperatures rise, the altitude at which clouds form can also rise. When clouds pass above the treetops instead of through them, the forest loses a crucial source of moisture even when annual rainfall totals remain high. Researchers featured in the PBS report said Monteverde’s yearly rainfall remains close to levels recorded 50 years ago. What appears to be changing is the length of the dry season and the number of days when mist and fog reach the vegetation.

The first plants to show the strain include epiphytes, which grow on trees without drawing nutrients from them. Orchids, bromeliads, mosses and ferns are among the epiphytes that cover Monteverde’s branches and act like living sponges. To study what might happen if those plants disappear, scientists removed the epiphytes from 10 trees and compared them with 10 untouched trees. Monitoring equipment measured temperature, humidity, leaf moisture, sunlight and wind inside the canopy.

The stripped trees became hotter and drier. Without the plants to capture and temporarily store water, rain moved through the canopy more quickly instead of being released gradually into the forest. The concern is that the process could feed on itself. Longer dry periods weaken or kill epiphytes. Their disappearance then leaves the remaining canopy warmer and less able to hold water, making other plants more vulnerable.

Earlier research supports concerns that Monteverde is receiving less dry-season moisture from mist. A study published in the Journal of Geophysical Research found that this decline has been observed since the mid-1970s. Researchers have examined both warming ocean temperatures and forest clearing at lower elevations as possible factors lifting the cloud base.

Computer modeling found that lowland deforestation may have reduced the amount of Costa Rican mountain forest covered by fog by between 5% and 13%, while raising afternoon cloud bases by roughly 25 to 75 meters (82 to 246 feet). The study cautioned that further clearing could push the clouds higher still.

The consequences extend beyond the mosses and orchids visitors see along Monteverde’s trails. Cloud forests regulate water, store carbon and provide habitat for amphibians, birds and plants that depend on cool, consistently damp conditions. The Monteverde Cloud Forest Preserve protects more than 4,100 hectares (10,000 acres) of forest. Conservation groups are also restoring cleared land on the Pacific slope with native trees, giving wildlife more connected habitat and helping the landscape retain water.

Scientists are not saying Monteverde will suddenly lose its forest. Their warning is that a cloud forest can change gradually even when conventional rainfall measurements appear normal. The amount of rain still matters, but so does whether the clouds continue reaching the trees.

World.title: Man charged after neighbour spots stolen washing machine at repair shop; says he sold it for $25
World.content:
Man charged after neighbour spots stolen washing machine at repair shop; says he sold it for $25

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City man accused of stealing his neighbour’s $700 washing machine has pleaded not guilty after telling the court that the owner had actually given him the old machine because it was not working and he later sold it for just $25.

Richmond Isaac Roberts, 51, appeared in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on a charge of theft involving a blue-and-white Acros washing machine belonging to a 63-year-old neighbor.

Roberts initially attempted to plead guilty with an explanation, but after hearing the prosecution’s allegations, he disagreed.

“No, that dah nuh how it happened,” Roberts told the court.

He claimed the man had given him the washing machine because it was no longer working and that he subsequently sold it to another man for $25 for parts.

Based on that explanation, the Magistrate entered an equivocal plea of not guilty on Roberts’ behalf and offered him bail of $1,000 plus one surety of the same amount.

Roberts, however, was unable to immediately secure his release because court records showed he still had outstanding fines from previous matters, including a 2023 controlled-drug possession case, another theft matter and a 2015 bicycle offence for riding without a bell.

The court informed Roberts that the outstanding fines had to be settled before he could process bail. When he was unable to pay them, warrants were prepared for him to serve the default prison terms, leaving him behind bars at the Belize Central Prison.

In the current theft case, Bodden told police that on August 22 he left the washing machine beside the back step of his home before going to work. When he returned that evening, the machine was gone.

The man later spotted what he believed was his washing machine at a business that repairs refrigerators and appliances. He said the person there told him the machine had been obtained from Roberts.

The maintains that he never gave Roberts permission to take or sell the washing machine and told police it had been in working condition.

Roberts is now expected to challenge the theft allegation in court.

World.title: Two men challenge loitering charge after police bust them on Freetown Road; Man says he was working undercover security
World.content:
Two men challenge loitering charge after police bust them on Freetown Road; Man says he was working undercover security

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Two Belize City men have pleaded not guilty to loitering after police accused them of remaining on Freetown Road despite being instructed to move along.

Roman Riverol, a security guard, and BTL software specialist Eli Elezor Obando appeared in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Friday, where they were jointly charged with loitering in a public place.

Police allege the men were on Freetown Road and failed to move quietly along when instructed to do so by separate police officers.

Both men challenged the allegation.

Riverol told the court he was not simply hanging around the area but was working undercover security for a Chinese businessman whose store had reportedly been affected by increased criminal activity.

He said he was deliberately not wearing a security uniform so he would not easily be identified as the person guarding the establishment. Riverol claimed he explained the situation to police, but officers did not accept his explanation.

Obando, meanwhile, told the court he had only been speaking with Riverol when police arrived. He said he initially left the area but later returned and was detained when police came back and found him there again.

Both men pleaded not guilty and were granted self-bail of $100 each.

They are due back in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on October 5, 2026.

The Magistrate reportedly warned both men of the consequences of failing to return to court, as self-bail is less commonly granted than bail secured through a surety.

World.title: Corozal businessman slapped with $94,015 in fines after massive illegal seafood bust
World.content:
Corozal businessman slapped with $94,015 in fines after massive illegal seafood bust

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Corozal businessman has been slapped with more than $94,000 in fines after pleading guilty to illegally importing hundreds of pounds of jumbo shrimp and tilapia fillets along with octopus into Belize.

Leslie Lizarraga, 34, appeared in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court alongside 51-year-old David Romano Arana of Consejo Village following a Fisheries Department operation on September 3.

Lizarraga pleaded guilty to three counts of illegal importation and was fined a total of $94,015, while Arana pleaded not guilty and the prosecution subsequently withdrew all three charges against him.

The case arose after Fisheries officers, assisted by police, intercepted a silver GMC Sierra pickup along the Hattieville-Boom Road following a brief pursuit.

Authorities say the vehicle initially turned around and sped away from officers before eventually losing control and ending up in a ditch.

A search reportedly uncovered seven boxes containing 335 pounds of jumbo shrimp, another 58 boxes containing 1,566 tilapia fillets weighing approximately 290 pounds, and a bag containing 14 pieces of octopus.

The Fisheries Department had previously confirmed the seizure, saying the seafood was suspected of having been illegally imported and that both the vehicle and products were taken into its custody. The department warned that unauthorized seafood imports can present food safety and phytosanitary risks and undermine legitimate businesses that comply with Belize’s import requirements.

After seeking a sentencing indication from the court, Lizarraga’s attorney, David McKoy, entered guilty pleas on his client’s behalf. The court took into account that Lizarraga was a first-time offender and had saved judicial time by pleading guilty, opting for fines rather than imprisonment.

Lizarraga was fined $5,000 for illegally importing the shrimp, another $5,000 for the tilapia and $5,000 for the octopus, along with court costs.

The heaviest penalty came from the 1,566 tilapia fillets, for which an additional fine of $50 per piece amounted to $78,300. The 14 pieces of octopus attracted a further $700 penalty.

The prosecution also applied for the forfeiture of the GMC Sierra used to transport the seafood. McKoy objected, telling the court that the pickup does not belong to Lizarraga and arguing that its owner must be given an opportunity to oppose its forfeiture.

The Magistrate agreed to adjourn the forfeiture application until the vehicle’s owner can be notified and heard. The pickup remains in Fisheries Department custody.

Fisheries officials have since said their intelligence indicates illegally imported seafood has been moving into Belize regularly and supplying businesses including resorts and supermarkets. The department says investigators are also tracing potential buyers of the illegal products.

World.title: Joseph Vaccaro committed to stand trial for Gaston Barrow murder after challenging witness evidence
World.content:
Joseph Vaccaro committed to stand trial for Gaston Barrow murder after challenging witness evidence

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Belize City taxi operator Joseph Gabourel Vaccaro has been committed to stand trial in the High Court for the 2025 murder of Gaston Barrow, despite telling the Chief Magistrate that three prosecution witnesses did not identify him as the shooter.

Vaccaro, 31, appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Monday for the conclusion of his preliminary inquiry, nearly a year after he was remanded on the murder charge.

During the hearing, the prosecution submitted more than 70 statements and other documentary evidence, including photographs, DVDs, chain-of-custody forms, warrants and a wanted poster.

Vaccaro challenged portions of the prosecution’s evidence, telling the court that three witnesses whose statements were included in the disclosure did not name him as the person who fired the fatal shots. He questioned why he was being prosecuted for murder if those witnesses had not identified him as the shooter.

The Chief Magistrate explained that the Magistrate’s Court was not conducting the murder trial and that Vaccaro would have the opportunity to challenge the prosecution’s evidence when the matter is heard before the High Court.

The matter ended in a paper committal, and Vaccaro was ordered to stand trial during the High Court session beginning October 7, 2026.

Vaccaro was originally arraigned on October 6, 2025 and remanded to the Belize Central Prison. In July, he received 154 pages of disclosure along with five CDs and photographs forming part of the prosecution’s case.

The charge stems from the September 28, 2025 shooting at the Old Belize compound along the George Price Highway.

Police said Barrow was travelling in the front passenger seat of a vehicle driven by Hance Card, with two women in the rear, when a gunman allegedly approached from the vicinity of a taxi and opened fire.

Barrow was fatally wounded, while Card was also shot but survived. Police later said Card declined to provide investigators with a statement.

Investigators reviewed surveillance footage from the Old Belize compound, which police said eventually led them to Vaccaro. Public reporting at the time said police believed the attack was gang-related and possibly connected to retaliatory violence.

Vaccaro remains on remand awaiting his High Court trial.

World.title: Nearly 400 police officers, undercover cops and drones deployed for Carnival; about 12 detained
World.content:
Nearly 400 police officers, undercover cops and drones deployed for Carnival; about 12 detained

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Nearly 400 police officers were deployed for Saturday’s Belize City Carnival Road March as authorities used uniformed officers, undercover personnel, drones and Coast Guard support to police the massive event.

ASP Stacy Smith said major events such as Carnival require advance operational planning because of the large crowds and the possibility that individuals may use those gatherings to target rivals.

Just under 400 officers were strategically deployed, including uniformed personnel, members of specialized operational units and undercover Special Branch officers.

Smith joked that some undercover personnel may even have been dressed in Carnival costumes.

Police also deployed drones along the route, which Smith said allowed officers to identify and intervene in disturbances before they escalated.

About 12 people were detained in connection with various disturbances, but police say the event generally concluded without any major security incident.

The Belize Coast Guard also assisted police because portions of the Carnival activity took place near the seafront.

The 2026 Road March began at Lord Rhaburn Plaza at Memorial Park and ended at the Marion Jones Sporting Complex.

Smith thanked the officers who worked the event as well as members of the public who cooperated with authorities.

World.title: Police say no extra officers deployed to Cayo despite drug tensions; technology and intelligence driving operations
World.content:
Police say no extra officers deployed to Cayo despite drug tensions; technology and intelligence driving operations

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The Belize Police Department says it has not deployed additional officers to Western Belize in response to recent drug-related violence, arguing that sustained operations and increased use of technology are already underway in the area.

ASP Stacy Smith said police have been concentrating operational resources in Cayo for some time and believe recent successes are partly the result of investment in technology and intelligence-led policing.

Police have previously linked violence in San Ignacio and Santa Elena to competition over the illegal drug trade and have said cocaine and crack cocaine are increasingly appearing among younger users and street-level dealers.

Last week, police reported that operations in Cayo had removed more than 35,000 grams of cannabis, 2,468 grams of cocaine, 1,253 grams of crack cocaine and 1,043 grams of methamphetamine from the streets. Police said those operations resulted in dozens of people being charged.

Smith said authorities remain interested in targeting major suppliers but stressed that street-level dealers are also part of the trafficking network.

She argued that disrupting retail sellers reduces the local market and, in turn, the incentive for larger quantities of drugs to enter the country.

Smith also noted that drugs do not only enter Belize by illicit aircraft, pointing to Belize’s land borders with Guatemala and Mexico. Police continue to use the Mobile Interdiction Unit in northern and western Belize to target suspected trafficking routes.

Two of five new pickup trucks recently provided to the Police Department have also been assigned to the Cayo District.

World.title: Police identify vehicle type in Brianna Myvett murder but still have no motive or suspects
World.content:
Police identify vehicle type in Brianna Myvett murder but still have no motive or suspects

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police say surveillance footage has helped investigators identify the make and model of a vehicle believed to have been involved in the murder of 20-year-old Brianna Myvett, but the vehicle did not carry licence plates and no motive has yet been established.

Myvett was shot and killed on Freetown Road on the night of August 31 while she was inside a Ford Escape with 24-year-old Alexander Carr, who was also shot and injured. Public reports described Myvett as a recent Wesley Junior College graduate, volleyball player and employee of the Belize Central Prison.

ASP Stacy Smith said investigators have retrieved several pieces of video footage and have been tracing the vehicle of interest in an effort to determine who entered or occupied it.

Two persons of interest were detained based on statements investigators received concerning a possible motive, but Smith said that line of investigation has so far yielded nothing concrete.

Police say neither Myvett nor Carr was known to police, and investigators have not determined whether Myvett, Carr or both were the intended targets.

“No motive has been established,” Smith said, adding that police are continuing to commit resources to the investigation.

Myvett was laid to rest on September 2.

World.title: NIP issued to pickup driver after Red Bank motorcycle crash kills 59-year-old man
World.content:
NIP issued to pickup driver after Red Bank motorcycle crash kills 59-year-old man

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have issued a Notice of Intended Prosecution to a female pickup driver following a fatal traffic accident in Red Bank Village that claimed the life of 59-year-old Nerry Campbell.

The collision occurred at about 10:45 a.m. on Saturday, September 5.

Police say Campbell was travelling on a motorcycle and was turning onto the Red Bank Road when a collision occurred with a pickup truck.

Campbell sustained serious injuries and was taken for medical treatment but succumbed shortly after 1:00 p.m.

Public reporting identified Campbell as a Guatemalan labourer living in Red Bank Village and identified the pickup as a Toyota Tundra driven by 30-year-old Deidra Jackson of Silk Grass. The collision reportedly occurred at the junction of Red Bank Road and the Thomas Vincent Ramos Highway.

Police have since issued Jackson a Notice of Intended Prosecution as the investigation continues.

World.title: Documentary on James Bond creator Ian Fleming to premiere at GoldenEye
World.content:
Portrait taken in the early 1960s of Ian Fleming, a British journalist, secret service agent, writer, whose most famous creation was the superhero James Bond, agent 007. (Photo: AFP)

Ian Fleming and the Curse of James Bond, directed by Adam Low, a new feature documentary exploring the life, imagination and enduring legacy of James Bond creator Ian Fleming, will premiere at GoldenEye, Fleming’s former Jamaican home, during the 80th anniversary year of the villa’s construction.

The documentary explores Fleming beyond the legend of 007, considering the contradictions, pressures and fascinations that shaped both the man and the charged literary world he created, according to a press release by Gross Media, which executive produced the project.

Presented at GoldenEye by Gross Media, the premiere weekend – November 19 to November 22, 2026 – brings together biography, place and mythology in a setting deeply connected to the Bond story.

“GoldenEye’s enduring legacy as a center of Jamaican art and creativity is rare and compelling,” said Gross Media founder David M Gross. “So much new has originated here and radiated outward — through music, painting, literature and the performing arts. Our film invites a new generation to come to Oracabessa, St Mary, to understand that legacy and be inspired by it.”

Built in a uniquely Jamaican architectural style, the iconic villa features whitewashed walls, wooden louvers and has no glass windowpanes.

Upon returning from espionage duties during World War II, Fleming built the villa in 1946 on Jamaica’s famed North Coast. GoldenEye became the creative sanctuary where he wrote each of the 12 James Bond nov els and the stories that introduced one of the most recognizable characters in modern popular culture.

Eight decades later, the property remains a living landmark: part legendary literary site, part cultural myth and an enduring symbol of Jamaica’s oversized place in the Bond story and the wider cultural world.

“Fleming built GoldenEye as a place where he could write, and every James Bond novel was written here. Eighty years later, it remains the spiritual birthplace of Bond. To screen a film that looks so closely at Fleming himself, during GoldenEye’s 80th year, is very special,” said Chris Blackwell, Founder, and Marika Kessler, CEO, Island Outpost.

Adam Low, the film’s director, said he was “determined to put Jamaica at the centre of the story” with the project.

“Even the Bond books not set there are infused with the island’s atmosphere, landscape and history. By including Jamaican voices — from Fleming’s longtime gardener Ramsay Dacosta to novelist Marlon James as well as Minister Olivia ‘Babsy’ Grange whose relative Aunt Violet was Fleming’s house manager — the film shows how deeply Jamaica shaped Fleming’s imagination and the world of Bond,” Low said.

“As Minister Grange says in the film, ‘Jamaica is the star of the Bond films,’ and the documentary makes a compelling case that without Jamaica, there would be no James Bond,” said Low, underlining the Jamaican connection.

The perspective of the film deepens the premiere’s connection to GoldenEye by positioning Jamaica not simply as Fleming’s retreat, but as a defining creative force behind Bond’s settings, sensibility and mythology.

“By weaving together Jamaican voices, landscapes and history, the documentary underscores the island’s central place in both Fleming’s imagination and the continuing cultural life of 007,” said film editor Joanna Crickmay.

According to the release, the film’s opening sequence features a moving benediction in the Rastafari tradition by author, journalist and cultural liaison Barbara Blake-Hannah, while driving the vibrant streets through Oracabessa, St Mary, en route to GoldenEye with Desmond Dekker & The Aces’ legendary rocksteady and reggae track “007 (Shanty Town)” on play.

The premiere film weekend will bring guests from around the world to the place where Fleming’s daily writing ritual helped launch the Bond phenomenon, the release stated, adding that the programme includes a screening at PlayScape, a cocktail party at the GoldenEye villa with a Jamaican jazz band, a classic Jamaican BBQ on Button Beach with members of the film’s crew and Ian Fleming-themed morning breakfasts: scrambled eggs, toast, guava jelly, local fruits and Blue Mountain coffee.

Together, the events offer guests a rare opportunity to experience the film in the setting most closely associated with Fleming’s creative life, according to the press release.

World.title: Stronger schools
World.content:
Education Minster Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon walks with students of Maud McLeod High School in Westmoreland where she filmed her back-to-school message to the nation.

After a school year battered by Hurricane Melissa, particularly in western Jamaica, but capped by improved results in the country’s major examinations, Education Minister Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon is looking to the new school year with optimism, pointing to increased investment, and stronger infrastructure as Jamaica pushes to transform its education system.

The scale of the challenge facing schools remains stark.

According to Morris Dixon’s back-to-school message, more than 688 schools were damaged by Melissa, 313 of them severely, while almost $26 billion is being spent on repairs and reconstruction. As she has repeatedly done in the past few weeks she acknowledged, however, that the work is not advancing as quickly as the Government would like.

Still, she said preparations were being made to get schools open, including contingency arrangements for institutions where repairs have not yet been completed.

“Thanks to the excellent work of our principals, boards, and the ministry team, we are working to have all schools open tomorrow. I have to thank all who have worked so hard over the summer and who have put in place contingency plans to support reopening even where repairs are not completed,” she said.

For Morris Dixon, however, rebuilding after Melissa is only part of the task.

The Government is entering the new school year with more than $835 million in operational support for schools, representing an average 55 per cent increase in funding. The minister said all schools received the first tranche of the increased funding in June, ahead of the reopening.

More than $1 billion is also being invested in educational resources, including workbooks, readers, textbooks, e-books, virtual learning solutions, and supplementary materials.

The increased spending comes against the backdrop of what Morris Dixon described as a strong finish to the last academic year, despite the disruption caused by the Category 5 storm.

“Despite the historic, once-in- a- 100-year devastation caused by the passage of Hurricane Melissa, we ended the last academic year with improved results across our major exams — PEP, CSEC and CAPE. Jamaica’s children did so well despite so much being thrown at them!” she said.

The minister is now betting on that resilience, alongside new investments, to drive further gains. In her speech she reminded the country of plans already in place.

Among the biggest initiatives is a $400-million investment in technical and vocational education at high schools. Technical high schools are to receive state-of-the-art laboratories in areas including autonomous robotics, renewable energy, virtual welding, electrical engineering, industrial controls, and optoelectronics.

The Government is also retooling science laboratories, while more than 150 satellite systems have been distributed to schools to improve Internet access, with additional devices being procured, particularly for rural institutions.

Morris Dixon said the hurricane recovery programme is similarly being used as an opportunity to improve schools beyond simply repairing the damage.

“Our Melissa reconstruction programme has not only presented an opportunity to make our schools more resilient, but it has also provided an opportunity to upgrade and renovate staffrooms for educators across Jamaica. The Staffroom Renovation Programme covers 74 institutions in the first phase, with work concentrated heavily in the parishes hardest hit by Melissa,” she said.

And while buildings, equipment and technology are central to the push, the minister also highlighted the needs of students outside the classroom.

More than 160,000 students are projected to benefit from the traditional cooked lunch programme, while another 69,000 students in the most challenged schools are expected to receive both breakfast and lunch. Meanwhile, 316 school cooks were trained and received range cook certification over the summer.

Psychosocial and psychological support, including trauma-informed services and Psychological First Aid, will also continue into the new academic year, after being intensified during the previous one.

Morris Dixon said the ambition extends beyond simply getting schools reopened and students back into classrooms.

“The ministry’s commitment is to continue transforming education so that every child, regardless of where they live or their circumstances, has a fair opportunity to learn, grow and succeed,” she said.

World.title: Sykes again makes case for judge-alone trials
World.content:
Chief Justice Bryan Sykes.

MONTEGO BAY, St James — Citing a far-advanced case — during the last circuit within the western end of the country— in which the jury had to be discharged, Chief Justice Bryan Sykes has again called for serious consideration to be given to judge-alone trials.

“After four weeks of trial, that was it. It was just waiting for addresses and the summation to be done [but] the jury had to be discharged,” he said during the 2026 Legal Year Western Region Assize Church Service at the West Jamaica Conference of Seventh-day Adventists in Mount Salem, St James, on Saturday.

In cases where juries are discharged Sykes’s preference is for the judge to then give a final verdict instead of having the matter drag on. He has consistently advocated for judge-alone trials in a bid to reduce case backlog and ensure that everyone accused of a crime is granted their constitutional right to a fair trial within a reasonable time. During the weekend church service he spoke of how a reliance on jury trials has impacted St James, particularly in relation to murder cases.

According to Sykes there were 170 cases before the court last circuit, and the perennial problem of finding individuals willing to serve as jurors persist.

“The judge was endeavouring to be as efficient as she could, actually running two to three trials at a time; and after four weeks of trial, [for] one of them, the jury had to be discharged,” said Sykes.

“The question is now, ‘Are we organising ourselves in a manner that justice can reach these 170 cases?’ Because it’s not just 170 persons because some of the cases have multiple defendants,” he added.

He noted that the numbers represent more than 200 people and impact not only those awaiting trial but also witnesses and relatives of the bereaved who have suffered great loss.

“We have to look again at the question of jury trials,” the chief justice urged.

Under the Criminal Justice (Administration) Act, which was amended by the Jury (Amendment) Act in 2015, the prosecution and the defence must agree, in writing, for an offence to be tried by a judge only.

As he has done in the past, Sykes on Saturday pointed to an opinion handed down by Jamaica’s highest court of final appeal, which he said should be utilised to guide the way forward.

“One of the most intriguing things to me is that the Privy Council has pointed to a solution for nearly four years now when the Adijah Palmer case went there,” he said, referencing the case of the individual widely known as dancehall artiste Vybz Kartel.

In 2024 the Privy Council overturned Kartel’s murder conviction based on its findings that the trial judge erred when, instead of discharging the entire jury, instead allowed the trial to continue with a juror who attempted to bribe others on the jury.

“What did they say? ‘If you’re going to have jury trials you can do it in such a manner that in the event that the jury must be discharged, then the trial can continue with the judge,” Sykes said of the Privy Council’s ruling in the Kartel case.

That would be a much easier approach than attempting to start over with a fresh panel of jurors or even adding alternates. Many individuals, for various reasons, shy away from serving as jurors.

On Saturday the chief justice made a fresh appeal for Jamaicans to do their civic duty and participate in the administration of justice.

“I dare say this is an appropriate place for me to repeat this again, ‘Show up when called to serve.’ So I am looking here at potential jurors who will, no doubt, be the first persons at the court in St James when you get the summons,” he quipped.

“You need to turn up and participate because our citizens — both those who are charged and those who are waiting to give evidence, those who have been the victim of violence — they need justice to be done, and you are a part of that process,” Sykes underscored.

He explained that the situation has become even more challenging given the impact on court facilities following the passage of last October’s Hurricane Melissa.

“A region does not fully recover with new buildings and new roofs, it recovers when it’s people also trust that they will be treated fairly, that their disputes will be heard, and that the law stands with them and not over them,” he told the gathering.

“Access to justice must reach every person in western Jamaica as surely as relief and rebuilding must,” he added.

Sykes pointed to the St James and Westmoreland parish court buildings as structures that have been impacted and are in need of urgent repair and redevelopment to serve the needs of the people. He noted that the St James Parish Court has for years had serious flooding issues. Despite these challenges, he urged members and partners of the legal fraternity who interact with the system to play their part in improving its efficiency.

“Justice restored in this region will not be the achievement of the judiciary alone, it depends on every arm of the profession pulling in the same direction. I ask that we examine our own practices,” he said.

“Too often the delay in our courts are not the faults of the bench. And I am not saying that the bench is never at fault, but what I am saying [is that] in many instances it is not the fault of the bench but documents come too late, incomplete, or not at all,” he lamented, adding that this must change.

World.title: Hot under the collar
World.content:
Airy Castle Primary School in St Thomaskarl mclarty

With intense heat expected to test students’ comfort, Airy Castle Primary Principal Dawn Graham is hoping conditions will not become a trigger for aggression this academic year.

“I’m… looking for a better school year than last year in terms of behaviour [because] that has been a concern, especially amongst our grade six students for last year. I’m hoping that the heat is not going to be a trigger to aggressive behaviour,” she told the Jamaica Observer during a visit to the school last week.

The heat was already severe enough to affect adults during a recent training session at the school. Graham is concerned about what conditions could be like once what she described as poorly ventilated classrooms are filled with children for extended periods.

“I sat in a training session with the teachers and the support staff and it was really hot. It was hot to the point that I know that at least two adults complained of severe headache, including myself… When those students are together in that space… I am [expecting we will be] seeing serious fatigue, especially in the afternoon and when the sun is really up,” she expressed.

The educator is counting on parents to keep students in check, despite the challenging circumstances.

“I’m hoping the parents are ready to give their support. I’m looking forward to an improved year, in especially, parent support,” said Graham.

In addition to keeping students cool, school officials will also have to keep an eye on their water supply.

St Thomas is among the parishes affected by water prohibition measures put in place to ration the commodity, as much of the country remains in the grip of a worrying dry spell. According to Graham, Airy Castle has experienced water problems in the past and they are watching closely to see whether the current conditions will place additional pressure on its supply.

“We will not act as though this is not a concern because the drought is upon us. We have already started to see the effects of the drought on the green areas,” she said.

The school currently has two full tanks, including one holding about 4,000 gallons, giving it a measure of protection as students return. Graham has a lot of confidence that support will be provided by the regional arm of the Ministry of Education if needed.

“What I am particularly impressed by is that in our region, they have been doing their checks and balances. The schools are already checked to see how many tanks are available, whether we are having difficulties with getting water for next week or storage. They have already checked that… so, for now, we are safe for starting,” she told the Observer.

But there is still the possibility of disruptions, and she would love to have more storage capacity.

“Should the piped water be affected, as it usually is sometimes, we are going to have serious problems,” Graham warned.

She explained that even before the current drought conditions, they have had challenges that have forced them to rely on trucked water.

“Water lock-offs are an issue here, mainly if the pump is broken or damaged, and that happens… about 40 per cent of the time. When it does happen, it is prolonged. Might be a month or more where you have to get trucked water sometimes, so it is a concern,” she said.

“I would think that we need to get more tanks in, which the ministry, as I said, they have been doing well at that by doing their checks and trying to put plans in place… We could do with another 2,000-gallon tank to be on the safe side; or another 4,000-gallon would be nice,” she added.

Despite concerns about the water supply and heat, Graham said Airy Castle is largely ready for the new school year, with about 90 to 95 per cent of preparations completed when the

Observer visited last Tuesday.

The remaining work involves basic infrastructure repairs, electrical work, and maintenance, which she said are being funded through grants from the education ministry.

World.title: Koffee makes waves with ‘Ova So’
World.content:
KOFFEE...there’s different energies that you’ll experience on the album, different genres, different feels of the music, and I think overall fans can expect a pretty cool, chill experience

By the time the sun began its descent over Wickie Wackie Beach on Friday, the shoreline had taken on a different kind of rhythm. Waves rolled quietly towards the sand, the evening breeze moved easily through the gathering and, against the picturesque backdrop of sea and sky, a specially invited crowd waited for Koffee to give them a taste of what comes next.

There was no sprawling concert stage or sea of thousands demanding her attention. Instead, the Grammy-winning artiste chose intimacy — a fitting setting for a musical reintroduction that appears to be unfolding on her own terms.

At the centre of Friday’s gathering was Ova So, Koffee’s latest single and another breadcrumb on the road towards her highly anticipated new album, due in October. The track was unveiled as part of a series of mini pop-up shows the reggae star has been using to reconnect with audiences ahead of the project, turning each appearance into both a performance and a preview of the musical chapter she is preparing to open.

For an artiste whose career once moved at whirlwind speed — from breakout sensation to Grammy winner and international stages in just a few short years — this latest chapter feels less like a race back into the spotlight and more like a carefully paced return. At Wickie Wackie, there was room for the music to breathe, for Koffee to meet her audience up close and, for one evening, allow a select few inside the world she has been quietly creating.

For Koffee, Ova So may feel particularly familiar to those who have been following her from the beginning.

“I think this is one of the songs dem weh me original fans dem ago love because I think it has a similar style to some of my earlier work like

Raggamuffin, using oldies samples and stuff like that,” she shared.

That familiarity, however, should not be mistaken for an indication that the forthcoming project will remain in one musical lane.

“There’s different energies that you’ll experience on the album, different genres, different feels of the music, and I think overall fans can expect a pretty cool, chill experience,” Koffee said.

Koffee’s latest musical exploits come after a brief hiatus, but as she readies a new project the entertainer is promising consistency. She outlined that her time away from the music scene allowed her to prepare herself mentally for the re-emergence she’s now experiencing.

“Fans can expect more presence and consistency from me,” she said. “I can definitely say that the time I took off the scene, I rejuvenated myself, refreshed myself, and just made sure my mind was in the right place to take on the road again.”

“I think I’m doing the best I’ve been doing my entire life, and I’m looking forward to experiencing even more and better,” she added.

World.title: Cops confident though traffic snarls expected in MoBay
World.content:
Motorists travelling along the West Green/Catherine Hall area of the under-construction Montego Bay Perimeter Road Project about noon on Saturday had to navigate dusty, uneven surfaces, while keeping an eye out for construction crew and heavy equipment. (Charmaine N Clarke)

MONTEGO BAY, St James — With the massive Western Water Resilience Project added, over the summer break, to the mix of work being done in and around this city, there is concern that there will be major traffic challenges today as thousands of students head out for the start of the new school term. Superintendent Eron Samuels, who leads the St James Police Division, is encouraging commuters to factor delays into their travel time.

“In light of all the work that is being done, we have already identified the areas of concern. For the pipeline project, that has been progressing smoothly [in terms of] how they have set up and organised themselves. What we will ask is that people leave out a little bit earlier so that they can make up time for the delays that they will have in that project. That is the one that we believe will cause a little bit more headache than the others,” he told the Jamaica Observer Friday.

Even as he stressed that he does not anticipate any major delays, he said he will have boots on the ground in that area today. Looking ahead to the evening rush hour, he is hoping commuters will take a staggered approach to road travel.

“If they have somewhere they can go and sit and relax for a little while until the traffic runs off, that will help to ease the congestion and ease the anxiety that they’ll face by being in traffic for extended periods,” said Samuels. “The truth is, we have more vehicles than the network of the roadwork can actually manage, so no matter what, the number of vehicles is just a challenge. So unless persons carpool or take public transportation, we will still see some issues as it relates to traffic… We have seen an increase in public transportation, the JUTC buses… so let us ask them to utilise those,” he encouraged.

Samuels and his team have amassed years of experience handling the back-to-school rush, and past traffic management plans have taken into account everything from protests to pothole-riddled roads.

Some may argue that this year is different.

Phase 1 of the US$450-million Western Water Resilience Project began along the Elegant Corridor in Rose Hall, St James, in June. Pipe-laying between Greenwood and Montego Bay is expected to last two years, with completion anticipated by summer of 2028. Work also continues on the US$354-million Montego Bay Perimeter Road which intersects the North Coast Highway at Ironshore, with its various sub-projects impacting traffic flow in the vicinity of Alice Eldemire Drive and Howard Cooke Highway, along with large residential communities in Bogue, Irwin, Cornwall Courts, and Salt Spring. In the Catherine Hall/West Green area, for example, traffic slowed to a crawl about midday Saturday as motorists navigated dusty, uneven surfaces while keeping an eye out for construction crew and heavy equipment.

The last deadline provided by the works ministry is for work on West Green Avenue to be completed this month. Samuels — who said he expects the bypass to open around the middle to the end of this school term — stressed that this will divert significant traffic away from the heart of the bustling city.

For now, based on how the project has been handled to date, he does not anticipate any issues when schools are once again in session. And even if things do not go as smoothly as he expects, he is confident his team can handle it.

“We will have enough personnel on the ground to monitor those. In the township itself, we’ll be putting police officers at the stop lights, as usual, to keep the traffic moving,” explained Samuels.

While he declined to divulge specific numbers regarding deployment, he acknowledged that there are staffing constraints which may impact how his team prevents and clears traffic snarls.

“There are never enough police officers, based on what we do and things that might happen, but we are flexible and we have shown that we have been managing the traffic situation,” he said.

Samuels noted that the division recently received an influx of additional traffic personnel, which paid off in smoother traffic flow since earlier in the year and positively impacted the previous school term. He said overall policing strategies for the city remain largely unchanged, with cops prepared to pivot as necessary.

He also confirmed that traffic personnel are strongly encouraged to wear body cameras.

“Our direct traffic police officers, most of them will be equipped. If they’re not equipped, it’s probably because we ran out of body cameras or if they have more than one police officer working at the same location. But we have been encouraging and monitoring our traffic police officers to wear their body cameras,” stated Samuels.

Confident that his team is ready for today, the St James divisional head pointed to an area of concern that is beyond their control: potholes. He described them as “major impediments” to smooth traffic flow.

“We have to look and see how the NWA [National Works Agency] or the [St James] Municipal Corporation can assist in ensuring that these holes are filled up or patched before the school year begins to fully flow,” he said.

While not all schools are expected to open today, full operations are anticipated by the end of the week. Samuels assured that police personnel will be out in their numbers to cover critical areas, monitoring the situation on a day-to-day basis to prevent recurring issues.

“All in all, we have made our plans and we’re satisfied that the plans can work,” the superintendent assured.

World.title: Expect ‘a little bit of discomfort’
World.content:
Some of the roofless teachers’ cottages are at the front of Knockalva Technical High School located at Ramble in Hanover is seen on WednesdayAnthony Lewis

RAMBLE, Hanover — Staff and students of Knockalva Technical High School here in this parish should not be surprised when they show up to school this morning and see that there is still work left to do to fix damage inflicted by last year’s Hurricane Melissa. During orientation last Tuesday, Principal Gregory Brown gave members of his team and parents a heads up that they will likely experience “a little bit of discomfort”.

He anticipates that when classes resume for the 800 students enrolled, this will delay work planned for some labs, bathroom facilities and re-installation of air-conditioning units.

“Some of those conversations are being had with the parents, that you’re going to experience… a little bit of displacement here and there. But it is far better than the children staying out. They have stayed out too long in our view. The parents and the staff, we are on board together to find a way to make the best use of the space we have to have all the children come [today] as we work to get back to some normalcy,” Brown told the

Jamaica Observer during a visit to the school last week.

He said that after four missed deadlines, repairs finally began on August 6 and there were mileposts along the way to help move the work along.

“We would have set deadlines for individual sections that they were doing, the different areas. So far, they have met the deadline for covering the roof, for resealing them…They have met the deadline for covering the canteen. I’m hoping they were sourcing material to cover the auditorium. If those things are in place, I think they’ll meet the deadline as well,” he said, his voice full of optimism.

“Overall though, I get the impression that we should be about 80 per cent complete by mid-October or roundabout there,” the educator added.

He explained that the remaining 20 per cent of work — such as cupboard replacement and AC installation — are things that will not have a significant impact on the school’s daily operations.

“Overall, the board and myself, we are kind of pleased at the rate at which they are going. It’s night and day, and the premix trucks are there. They come regularly,” stated Brown, who had high praise for the Ministry of Education and its agency, the National Education Trust (NET).

However, while the ongoing repair work is not a major worry, he is concerned about lingering challenges with staff housing and a shortage of water.

Knockalva Technical High is supplied by piped water from the National Water Commission’s (NWC) facility in Chester Castle. While the region sits in a watershed area, the school normally receives water once or twice a week. Brown noted that drought conditions have further reduced supplies.

“An area that is of even greater concern… is water. It’s really something that is now popping up and we are giving it serious attention,” he said.

Before last year’s Category 5 storm damaged vital equipment, the school used to do rain water harvesting.

“Our science department would treat the water [by using] training that they had with NWC. But even though we’re having rains now, the harvesting facility was damaged and since they have worked on the roof, it takes a little while to get back that up,” stated Brown.

Before the storm, the school’s water harvesting system included 25 metal and black tanks. That number has been reduced to 15 tanks which need up to 5,000 gallons daily to operate effectively. Last Tuesday, the school received 10,400 gallons of trucked water that was expected to last them four days.

“The water now is just as critical a thing as full completion [of the repairs]. It’s concerning to us because it’s expensive to get the water in. [Water trucked by] the Government and NWC alone cannot provide the amount of water that we need because they have to go to the police station, they have to go to other schools, they have to go to so many other places. So we too, through our private contractor, have to stop the gap that exists. We are doing so but I don’t know how long we can do that because it’s an expensive venture,” said a worried Brown.

He also has to grapple with fallout from the damage Hurricane Melissa did to the school cottage. Now, teachers who would have stayed there are forced to commute roughly 40 miles daily.

“It’s not easy to get accommodation in the area because most of the houses and the persons who used to provide these accommodations to our staff members are suffering [hurricane] damage as well. It forces our teachers to travel. I have 15 that were living on plant [the cottage] having to travel from as far as Santa Cruz [in St Elizabeth],” explained Brown.

But even with almost a year of challenges, his teachers have put in the work and that was reflected in students’ performance.

“I can’t commend the teachers enough because this year, the exam passes are 50 per cent better than the year before. Some of the teachers who are travelling from as far as Santa Cruz are getting 100 per cent passes in the CSEC [Caribbean Secondary Education Certificate] exams. The effort and the commitment are beyond all contestation,” Brown said proudly.

World.title: EL NIÑO AT PLAY!
World.content:
Kivann Salmon (right) of Excelsior High School falls after a challenge by Kevon Adlam of Tivoli Gardens High School during the ISSA Manning Cup football match at Excelsior on December 2, 2025. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

WITH the schoolboy football season underway for the next three months, sports medicine specialist Dr Winston Dawes is urging relevant stakeholders to exercise extreme caution to prevent serious issues among players as it relates to the El Niño phenomenon.

The under-19 competition kicked off on Saturday with the opening games of the ISSA daCosta Cup first round, with the Manning Cup set to begin on Wednesday.

However, the players will have to deal with the higher-than-usual temperatures caused by El Niño, a complex weather pattern that results from variations in winds and sea surface temperatures.

Although it has affected the island over the summer months with temperatures approaching near 40 degrees Celsius, the Meteorological Service of Jamaica says the worst effects could last through to November. After seeing this week’s temperature map, senior meteorologist Romayne Robinson said outdoor activities such as physical education classes should “end before 10 or not take place at all”.

Dawes says dehydration and heat stroke are two of the main threats the players will face, especially with the fields constantly absorbing heat. However, he told the Jamaica Observer that these risks can be reduced by hydrating long in advance.

“You have to start from the evening before, whereby you drink tons of water and electrolytes; have glucose; have a carbohydrate-rich meal, simple carbohydrates; then throughout the morning you would drink tons of fluid so that you enter the match fully hydrated,” Dawes said.

ISSA President Keith Wellington says they have put measures in place to ensure the students are taken care of.

“The competition rules speak to these mitigating factors and what are some of the things we expect. Obviously we’ll have a policy of not playing double-headers where the teams have to be playing at 1 o’clock in the afternoon,” he said.

“We are going to be mindful of the issue of safeguarding of our student athletes. Even from a management perspective, we have said this year that each team must have a safeguarding officer — that is somebody who is not a coach, who is not a part of the technical staff, maybe just a teacher who has no interest at all in football but has interest in the duty of care for our students. So yes, we are mindful of the El Niño effect but [at the same time we are] just generally ensuring that our students are taken care of.”

Football’s world governing body, FIFA, introduced mandatory hydration breaks during this summer’s World Cup to combat the heat in the United States, Mexico and Canada, though it was criticised due to its commercial aspect.

The ISSA Competitions Committee revealed that hydration breaks will be implemented but won’t be mandatory. Instead, their occurrence will depend on the specific conditions on match day.

Dawes, though, says players must be given the chance to hydrate at any given point during the game.

“Even if you don’t have the formal break, they should allow the players to be able to come to the sidelines and drink something. Whether it’s for a throw-in or a kick, they could allow 15 seconds for people to drink,” he said.

“The coaches are going to have to monitor the kids, speak to them about everything, and that if the referees, coaches or medical personnel see something happening, they should have the right to assess the player and also call for rehydration. It means that the adults who are responsible for organising the game have got to be on the alert for anything untoward.”

Dawes, who also served as president of the Jamaica Football Federation, says referees should also exercise some leniency as hydration breaks should not be viewed as a time-wasting tactic.

“It’s not time-wasting to have people come and take a quick drink,” he said. “Time-wasting is something different; we have people who take one minute for a throw-in or a goal kick or kicking away the ball — that’s time-wasting. What you want to do is protect the players from overexertion, which creates problems.”

World.title: Mobilité : l’Europe doit passer des objectifs aux conditions de leur réalisation
World.content:
Premier exemple : le poids lourd. 78 % du fret terrestre européen passe par la route : presque tout ce qui remplit nos rayons a voyagé en camion. Pour électrifier ces flux, la technologie est là, le cadre aussi ; le nœud est économique. Surcoût à l’achat, valeur résiduelle incertaine, bornes de recharge à déployer, raccordements électriques trop lents, attentisme face à une technologie qui progresse vite : aucun acteur ne peut porter seul ces risques. La réponse consiste à mieux les répartir, voire à transformer des risques pour les uns en opportunités pour les autres. Location de la batterie, garantie des valeurs résiduelles, mutualisation de la recharge, sécurisation des volumes par contrat : l’écosystème dispose déjà d’une partie des solutions. L’action publique devient décisive là où le marché ne peut agir seul, ou pas assez vite, notamment sur les raccordements électriques et l’interopérabilité. Elle doit aussi rassurer sur la fermeté du chemin : non pas en généralisant les contraintes, mais en rendant la trajectoire crédible, en facilitant l’amorçage des transformations volontaires, et en accompagnant ceux qui prennent les premiers risques. Ce sont eux qu’il faut aider, avant de laisser les suiveurs rejoindre un marché devenu lisible et désirable. L’Europe ne doit pas revoir sa destination à chaque difficulté d’exécution, car rien ne décourage plus l’investissement que l’instabilité des règles ; elle doit créer les conditions permettant de l’atteindre. Faute de quoi l’incertitude sur le passage à l’échelle nourrit une contestation du cap lui-même. Le choix : répartir le risque pour créer le marché, ou rester trop longtemps prisonniers du diesel.

Deuxième exemple : la petite voiture populaire. L’Europe en a fait des icônes : la 2 CV, la Fiat 500, la Coccinelle. Puis nos voitures ont grossi : certains modèles pèsent désormais deux fois plus que leur ancêtre du même nom, et leur prix a suivi la même pente. Aujourd’hui la voiture électrique européenne reste hors de portée d’une grande partie des ménages. Nous avons commencé par le premium, subventionné les SUV, en espérant que les coûts descendent ensuite ; pendant ce temps, une déferlante de petites voitures électriques asiatiques, abordables et produites à grande échelle, se prépare à occuper l’espace que nous choisissons, par défaut, de laisser ouvert. La Commission a pris le problème de front en proposant une catégorie dédiée aux véhicules électriques compacts, avec des incitations pour ceux produits en Europe. C’est une avancée. Nous pensons qu’il faut aller plus loin, parce que tout s’y joue à la fois : la souveraineté industrielle, le pouvoir d’achat et l’écologie. C’est l’ambition du projet Pop Car, que nous menons avec une coalition d’industriels et d’experts : une voiture mieux dimensionnée dans sa masse, sa batterie et son coût complet d’usage, sobre, abordable, sans rien céder sur la sécurité ni la désirabilité. Là encore, ne pas vouloir contraindre tout le monde à basculer au même rythme, mais sécuriser une offre européenne qui amorcera le marché et laisser l’adoption s’élargir lorsque prix, usage et confiance seront réunis. La question est celle-ci : quelle voiture électrique un ménage européen pourra-t-il s’offrir demain, et où sera-t-elle produite ? Le choix : refaire de l’entrée de gamme un segment stratégique, ou la laisser se jouer ailleurs.

Troisième exemple : l’intelligence artificielle. Elle orchestre une part croissante de nos mobilités. Elle oriente les itinéraires de millions de véhicules, arbitre des flux entiers de circulation, répartit des ressources rares : le temps, l’espace public, les chargements, l’énergie. Depuis le 2 août 2026, l’AI Act impose ses premières obligations de transparence à certains systèmes. Nécessaire, mais cela ne dit pas ce que l’IA doit optimiser. L’IA exécute la consigne. Elle ne décide pas seule de ce qui compte. Faut-il privilégier la vitesse, l’efficience ou l’écologie ? Le coût pour l’opérateur ou l’accessibilité pour tous ? Ces priorités ne s’imposent pas d’elles-mêmes : ce sont des choix collectifs, qui s’écrivent dans le logiciel, et engagent autant nos mobilités qu’une infrastructure physique. Notre conviction : toute IA déployée dans la mobilité devrait démontrer son gain net — carbone, coût pour l’usager, accessibilité — et non le seul temps gagné. Ici aussi, le régulateur a un rôle décisif : fixer la boussole collective sans étouffer l’innovation, donner confiance aux pionniers, puis faciliter la diffusion des solutions utiles. Le choix : écrire la consigne collectivement, ou subir les règles opaques que d’autres auront écrites pour nous.

Trois exemples, un même fil : une transition réussit lorsque ceux qui doivent la rendre réelle ont intérêt et capacité à le faire. Familles, transporteurs, opérateurs, industriels : face au prix, au financement ou à l’investissement, tous pèsent le même type d’arguments. Mais tous ressentent aussi que notre modèle économique épuise la planète. Notre pari européen est de le réinventer par l’alignement volontaire des intérêts, et non par un dirigisme excessif. En démocratie, la puissance publique fixe une destination ; elle ne peut, seule, rendre le trajet possible. Il faut aussi donner à chacun les moyens, l’intérêt et la confiance nécessaires pour s’y engager librement.

Poser les contraintes sur la table, mettre les désaccords au travail, construire des trajectoires communes : c’est ce que nous faisons chez Movin’On, et ce que nous porterons les 8 et 9 octobre à Paris, lors de notre Summit. L’Europe a longtemps débattu de la destination. Elle doit maintenant organiser le voyage. Cela suppose une puissance publique ferme sur le cap, utile dans l’amorçage, attentive aux pionniers, puis confiante dans la capacité des acteurs à suivre lorsque les conditions sont réunies. C’est l’heure des choix.

Gaël Quéinnec

Directeur général de Movin’On

World.title: Draghi Report or Hugging Face: who will win the tech race?
World.content:
When a swarm of AI agents decided to hack the computation company Hugging Face in July, it took them six days. That event became a case study on how, and how fast, artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping both economic and power dynamics worldwide. When Mario Draghi published his report on how to re-establish European competitiveness, it took 729 days for Brussels to realize that only a fraction of his recommendations had been enacted. Tomorrow will mark the second anniversary of the report’s presentation and, according to draghiwatch.eu, only 15.7 percent of his recommendations have been fully implemented so far.

Tech and telecoms policy might have lost the “Draghi spirit”

In digital and tech, the number of fully implemented recommendations is currently even lower: only 6.4 percent. Draghi made a point of putting technology at the core of EU reform, and zoomed in on telecoms as a critical sector to deliver tech sovereignty and growth for future decades to come. Why? Because 5G, fiber and future 6G networks are the backbone of our economies and societies at a time in which economic growth is driven by technology.

As to the connectivity sector, less than half of Draghi’s telecom recommendations have been picked up in ongoing reforms and policy strategies. None has been implemented yet. Worse, the recommendations that have moved forward so far are largely cost-creating for the industry, such as technology bans in 5G or forced phase-outs of copper networks. The measures that would directly boost investment remain limited, for now, mainly to spectrum proposals; more on this below. That implementation gap matters because the technologies now moving fastest are precisely the ones that depend on Europe’s connectivity foundations. AI, cloud, defense tech and satellite connectivity are no longer separate policy files: they are becoming one industrial race.

Four fights reshaping connectivity (and tech leadership) today

Since Draghi’s report was published in 2024, innovation in connectivity has moved fast. The first fight is helping Europe claim its slice of the AI boom. Telecom operators are doing their part: data must move between AI data centers and back to users, and advanced 5G and future 6G networks can help industry turn AI into productivity gains. A German manufacturing plant or an Italian port using 5G and AI applications should be able to compete with Chinese or American peers.

Worse, the recommendations that have moved forward so far are largely cost-creating for the industry, such as technology bans in 5G or forced phase-outs of copper networks.

The second fight is creating a healthy sovereign cloud market. Many telecom operators are already responding to the demand from European businesses and public administration to provide sovereign cloud offers.

Another crucial fight is the one for developing more defense tech capabilities in Europe. Here, the synergies between defense companies and the telecom sector are becoming ever clearer, as keeping Europeans safe now requires advanced and secure communications. Just think of drones: telcos are already deploying services to keep our public spaces safe from malicious drones.

Finally, the fight for tech leadership also takes to space: Europe rightly has the ambition to get into the satellite connectivity game rather than leaving it only to others. Here, a recent positive satellite spectrum decision by the European Commission might help build leadership over time.

Four reforms that will decide whether Europe catches up

The European telecom sector is a regulated one and its health has downstream effects on the whole digital economy. This is why Europe can only win in tech when it completes the deep telecom reforms suggested by Draghi. Our view is that this depends on at least four major policy actions.

First, we need scale. Europe’s telecom markets remain too fragmented, with many operators too small to invest at the scale needed for advanced networks and dramatically improved customer experience. Consolidation therefore becomes a necessary tool, both in-market and across markets, to create stronger operators able to invest, innovate and interact with major global AI, chip and platform companies. The review of the EU Merger Guidelines, and its practical application in telecom cases, will play a crucial role here.

Second, we need a new telecom rulebook. The Digital Networks Act (DNA) is currently being reviewed by the European Parliament and member states. So far, the Commission’s main material improvement for 5G and 6G investment is the proposal to make spectrum licenses unlimited. Yet, troubling signals from co-legislators suggest that even this improvement could be watered down. If that happens, the DNA would lose the one positive measure that analysts and investors have identified so far. Other areas that should be tackled are: deregulating the current heavy-handed access regime, which currently prevents a rush to invest in fiber; removing the introduction of mandated switch-off of copper networks, which might end-up unintendedly harming consumers and removing their freedom of choice; and materially improving the space for telecom innovation, with clearer rules on specialized services and simplified service regulation.

Europe can only win in tech when it completes the deep telecom reforms suggested by Draghi.

Third, we must defend security with better tools than some of those suggested in the Cybersecurity Act (CSA). Unless improved, the current CSA will impose major costs, estimated at €30-40 billion by GSMA Intelligence, on telecom operators and their customers, effectively contradicting other pro-investment policy objectives. De-risking connectivity is worthy, however, we have serious doubts that this can be done simply by imposing an indiscriminate technology ban, while we would need a proportionate and truly risk-based approach. What about compensation, as the U.S. did? What about the investment capacity of the sector? What about unintended effects on consumers? Things are still not well-thought through.

Fourth, we need a Cloud and AI Development Act that strengthens Europe’s sovereignty, competitiveness and resilience in practice. The starting point in the Commission draft is good: the ultimate goal should be to accelerate Europe’s cloud and AI capacity, while creating the right conditions for demand, investment, deployment and scale.

The time that separates the presentation of the Draghi Report from today’s underwhelming implementation is 729 days. In the same timespan, AI agents can generate 120+ Hugging Face hacking scandals. If we are to win the race, Europe needs good quality legislation, bold one. And it needs it faster.
