It is not yet a fully fledged route-shaper, but it is steadily behaving like one—using new routes not to eliminate dependence, but to distribute it more strategically.

From concentrated dependence to managed interdependence

Every export option depends on another state, infrastructure operator, or external market. Self-reliance is not realistic. Kuchins nevertheless argues that Astana can “reduce concentration of its dependence on Russia.”

Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Energy reported 73.4 million tons of oil exports during the first eleven months of 2025. Separately reported full-year route data show 64.8 million tons transported through the CPC, 9.3 million through Atyrau–Samara, 3.5 million through Aktau, 1.1 million through Atasu–Alashankou toward China, and approximately 100,000 by rail. Of the 78.8 million tons accounted for in this route-level data, approximately 94% moved through the two Russian corridors. Kazakhstan therefore possesses several export routes, but its portfolio remains highly asymmetrical.

Herein lies its greatest oil-policy shift: managed interdependence. This means distributing export relationships so that no transit state possesses overwhelming influence over Kazakhstan’s market access. Each direction performs a different function.

And at the moment, Kazakhstan is assessing four directions—some mainstay, some new.

The Russian route

The CPC will remain dominant because it offers unmatched capacity, established infrastructure and lower costs. Kuchins and Roubanis expect structural dependence to persist through 2030. Following the Tengiz expansion, Kazakhstan may become more dependent on the CPC in the short term even as its long-term strategy diversifies. Diversification does not require abandoning the CPC; it requires making an interruption less damaging.

The Trans-Caspian route

BTC could absorb Kazakh crude as Azerbaijani production declines, while Baku–Supsa could provide another outlet. Neither would match CPC volumes, but together they would widen access to global buyers.

Europe also has a stake in this.

The European Union imported 52.4 million tons of Kazakh crude just in 2024, making Kazakhstan its third-largest external supplier. If Europe wants westward diversification, it must help make projects bankable through financing and long-term commitments. Brussels and its partners are therefore mobilizing 10 billion euros to improve transport connections with Central Asia. According to Roubanis, “building ties with the region in the short run is necessary for the EU’s long-term positioning.” The push indicates that Trans-Caspian connectivity is not just a Kazakh interest, but one shared by the whole region.

The Chinese route

China may offer the easiest immediately available opportunity to reduce dependence on Russia. The Kazakhstan–China pipeline transported 19.5 million tons in 2025, but that included domestic deliveries and Russian transit. Direct Kazakh crude exports through Atasu–Alashankou were planned to be 1 million tons in 2025, compared to the more than 11 million tons per year flowing with non-Kazakh suppliers.

China remains a credible expansion market and willing financier. Yet the fastest way to reduce Russian dependence could deepen dependence on China. Moriyasu similarly argues that Kazakhstan does not want to exchange one concentrated dependency for another. Unlike the Trans-Caspian route, China provides access to one principal market rather than multiple global buyers.

The Southern route

A corridor through Iran—possibly toward Pakistan and India—could be compelling but faces formidable political and economic obstacles. But it should not be dismissed altogether.

Moriyasu suggests that “Iran offers Central Asia one of its shortest routes to warm-water ports.” Although current geopolitical conditions severely constrain this option, he argues that “infrastructure Kazakhstan builds today will still be operating decades from now. Astana should therefore avoid making long-term infrastructure decisions on the assumption that today’s geopolitical map is permanent.”

The southern route’s present value lies in preserving a long-term option, not in providing a realistic alternative before 2030.

From east to west and north to south, Kazakhstan is not moving from dependence to independence. It is moving from one dominant dependency toward a deliberately balanced portfolio of interdependence.

A more advanced role, but not autonomy

Kazakhstan’s transformation should not be measured by whether the CPC ceases to dominate. By 2030, it will likely remain the principal corridor as Trans-Caspian volumes rise incrementally and eastbound capacity becomes more important amid regional instability and escalation. The resulting portfolio will be broader, though still asymmetrical.

The strategy is itself an upgrade—a threefold one. Resilience is becoming the objective, route-shaping the emerging function, and managed interdependence the organizing principle.

Looking forward, Kazakhstan’s strategic upgrade lies not in escaping geography, but in developing the infrastructure, partnerships and political leverage needed to manage geography more effectively.

The author is Joseph Shumunov, a Non-Resident Research Fellow at the Topchubashov Center in Baku, Azerbaijan, and a Fellow at Nightingale Intelligence.

Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the position of The Astana Times.

World.title: Former Georgian prosecutor general becomes commander of Russian military unit
World.content:
Former Georgian prosecutor general Otar Partskhaladze, who now lives in Russia and is known as Otar Romanov-Partskhaladze, will lead an international military unit formed to take part in the war against Ukraine.

Russia’s state-run news agency TASS reported this on 7 September, citing Partskhaladze himself.

Former Georgian prosecutor general Otar Partskhaladze, known in Russia as Otar Romanov-Partskhaladze. The photograph was shared by Partskhaladze’s friend Mamuka Pipia.

TASS describes Partskhaladze as a “veteran of the special military operation”. In an interview with the agency, he linked the creation of the unit to the Second World War and relations between the Russian and Georgian peoples.

“It was Russian Mikhail Yegorov and Georgian Meliton Kantaria who raised the Victory Banner over the Reichstag in 1945. One in four of my compatriots fought for freedom. I am certain that, as then, the symbol of the enemy’s defeat will once again be raised by a Russian and a Georgian.

“Our like-minded supporters, who advocate uniting our peoples and countries and defending traditional family values, have formed the international ‘St George’ unit,” the former prosecutor told TASS.

Partskhaladze explained that the unit’s name refers to the 1783 Treaty of Georgievsk, which he says played an important role in the history of the Georgian people. The treaty brought the eastern Georgian kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti under the protection of the Russian Empire.

Partskhaladze also says the new unit’s main task is “to finish the fight against the evil that threatens not only us, but the whole world”.

The former prosecutor says he decided to fight on Russia’s side and has helped Russian troops and people in the so-called Donetsk People’s Republic, as well as in Russia’s Kursk, Bryansk and Belgorod regions, with his team since the start of the “special military operation”.

“Today, as Russia fights Western pressure to preserve its identity, traditions, language and culture, I am ready to help my homeland achieve all the goals set by its leader,” TASS quoted Otar Partskhaladze as saying.

Who is Otar Partskhaladze?

Otar Partskhaladze became Georgia’s prosecutor general in November 2013, after the current ruling Georgian Dream party came to power. But he remained in the post for just 47 days and resigned on 30 December that year.

His resignation followed a scandal over his criminal conviction for theft in Germany. Partskhaladze confirmed that he had been convicted, but claimed that the case concerned resisting police rather than theft.

After leaving the prosecutor general’s office, Partskhaladze moved into business. For many years, however, he was considered an influential figure close to the inner circle of ruling party founder Bidzina Ivanishvili. Ivanishvili himself has said that Partskhaladze is a close friend of his son, Bera Ivanishvili. Bera Ivanishvili is the godfather of Partskhaladze’s grandson.

In 2017, Partskhaladze was accused of assaulting Lasha Tordia, who was then head of Georgia’s State Audit Office. Tordia linked the attack to an investigation by the Audit Office into ties between Tbilisi City Hall and a company owned by Partskhaladze. In 2021, the Tbilisi City Court acquitted Partskhaladze in the case.

Partskhaladze later obtained Russian citizenship and has lived in Russia in recent years.

He subsequently changed his surname to Partskhaladze-Romanov. According to information JAMnews obtained from open sources, he also has business interests in Russia.

In September 2023, the US imposed sanctions on Partskhaladze. According to the US State Department, Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) worked with Partskhaladze to influence Georgian society and politics in favour of Russia. The State Department says Partskhaladze worked with FSB officer Alexander Onishchenko, who also helped him obtain Russian citizenship.

After the sanctions were imposed, Georgian banks initially froze Partskhaladze’s accounts. However, after Georgian Dream leaders criticised the decision, the National Bank of Georgia changed its rules on implementing sanctions and restored Partskhaladze’s access to his accounts.

In October 2023, then-Georgian President Salome Zourabichvili stripped Partskhaladze of his Georgian citizenship.

In 2025, the UK also sanctioned Partskhaladze for supporting Russia’s war against Ukraine.

Partskhaladze is currently a defendant in a criminal case in Georgia. In December 2025, the Interior Ministry named him as the organiser of the killing of businessman Levan Dzhangveladze. According to the ministry’s account, Partskhaladze led an organised criminal group and ordered the murder of Dzhangveladze. He was charged in absentia and placed on an international wanted list.

As it turns out, none of this has stopped Russia’s state-run news agency from interviewing him.



Otar Partskhaladze to lead a military unit

World.title: Armenian and Turkish business leaders call for borders to reopen. Is it likely to happen?
World.content:
Armenian-Turkish business forum in Yerevan

Against the backdrop of a two-day business forum held in Yerevan with the participation of business representatives from Armenia and Turkey, debate over normalising Armenian-Turkish relations and reopening the border between the two countries has intensified in Armenian society.

Following the forum, the Union of Manufacturers and Businessmen of Armenia and the Van Chamber of Commerce and Industry issued a joint statement. The two countries’ business leaders called for the borders to reopen, border crossing points to resume operations and procedures for crossing the border to be simplified for both sides.

“Reopening the border crossing points would not only boost trade, but also mark an important step towards normalising relations. It would strengthen contacts, promote economic cooperation and build mutual trust between the peoples of the two countries. Opening the borders is crucial to unlocking the region’s economic potential in trade, investment, tourism and cultural exchange,” the statement said.

In an interview with JAMnews, political analyst Robert Ghevondyan said: “Under normal circumstances, developing economic and trade ties would have a significant impact on the process of reopening the borders. But our situation is not normal.” He was referring in particular to Azerbaijan’s enormous influence over Turkey through various means, including economic leverage.

“Yes, such initiatives provide a positive boost, at least at a psychological level. But for substantial changes to take place, the political issues must first be resolved. Above all, we need to focus on resolving relations with Azerbaijan,” Ghevondyan said.

From increasing trade to reopening the border: business leaders issue joint statement

Eighty representatives of the Van Chamber of Commerce and Industry travelled to Yerevan to attend the business forum. The two sides discussed opportunities for trade and investment, and explored prospects for closer cooperation between their business communities.

Business representatives described the forum as a “significant step” towards normalising relations and developing economic cooperation between Turkey and Armenia:

“The business community can make a significant contribution to building relations based on mutual understanding, trust and shared economic interests, regardless of borders and political differences. We believe that stronger economic and trade ties between Turkey and Armenia would contribute significantly to the economic and social development not only of the two countries’ business communities, but also of border regions, as well as Van and Yerevan.”

They said reopening the border would be crucial not only to boosting trade but also as an important step towards normalising relations:

“Van could become a natural trade and logistics bridge between Turkey and the Caucasus. Strengthening economic ties between Van and Yerevan could help develop regional trade and build greater understanding between the two peoples.”

On 3-4 September, Yerevan hosted a two-day business forum attended by representatives of the Armenian and Turkish business communities. The forum took place as part of the EU programme “Supporting the normalisation of Armenian-Turkish relations: strengthening cross-border ties”. Its aim was to bring together business and government representatives from the two countries to explore new forms of cooperation and build trust.

Comment

Political analyst Robert Ghevondyan says that despite the lack of diplomatic relations between Armenia and Turkey, trade ties between the two countries have long been established. However, these ties exist at the business level rather than between the governments.

He says there is now active work under way to normalise relations, which is also helping to develop economic ties further:

“Reopening the border could provide a major boost to further progress in this direction. We hope the border will open soon and that we will see the results.”

Ghevondyan notes that Turkey has already lifted its ban on direct exports to Armenia:

“Turkish companies can now file customs declarations directly for exports to Armenia and sell their goods there. As a result, Armenian and Turkish businesses no longer need intermediaries.”

At the same time, Ghevondyan points out that goods are transported through Georgia. Transit costs will therefore remain in place until the Armenian-Turkish border opens.

According to the political analyst, the next step is to reopen the border. This could lead to a major increase in economic ties.

Robert Ghevondyan says he cannot predict exactly when the border will open. But he hopes it will happen “as soon as possible”. He also stresses that reopening the border depends on the normalisation of Armenian-Azerbaijani relations:

“Azerbaijan sees the closed border with Turkey as a lever for putting pressure on Armenia. Once Azerbaijan decides that it no longer needs this leverage, the Turkish border will most likely open.”

As for whether the signing of an Armenia-Azerbaijan peace agreement could influence the process, Ghevondyan is not convinced that this would be the decisive factor:

“There is a possibility that even if a peace agreement is signed, Azerbaijan could ask its Turkish partners not to open the border. In that case, the border will remain closed.

“But there is also a possibility that no peace agreement will be signed, but Azerbaijan will no longer ask its Turkish partners to keep the border closed. In that case, the border will open.”

Speaking about Azerbaijan’s influence over Turkey, the expert listed the following factors:

Baku’s investments worth billions of dollars in Turkey;

the personal ties between Aliyev and Erdogan;

perceptions among Azerbaijani and Turkish societies.

“When Turkey opened the border for 10 days to allow humanitarian aid from Armenia to reach Syria, there was discontent in Azerbaijani society. This affected the decision-making circles in Turkey,” he said.

At the same time, Ghevondyan says Turkey does not even try to hide the extent of Azerbaijan’s influence:

“At meetings at different levels, Turkish partners say directly: ‘We have no problem with opening the border, but our Azerbaijani partners must not object.’”

Context

Turkey officially recognised the Republic of Armenia in 1991. But the two countries still have no diplomatic relations. In 1993, Turkey unilaterally closed its air and land borders with Armenia. The air border reopened in 1995, according to the Armenian Foreign Ministry website, “under pressure from the international community”.

Talks on normalising Armenian-Turkish relations intensified after the second Karabakh war. Although the normalisation process is taking place on a bilateral basis, Turkey coordinates the negotiating agenda with Azerbaijan.

In December 2021, Yerevan and Ankara said they were ready to take steps towards normalising relations. The two countries appointed special representatives to begin negotiations.

At the beginning of 2026, Armenian media reported that the border between Armenia and Turkey would open on 1 February to citizens of third countries and holders of diplomatic passports. The two countries’ special representatives had agreed on this in July 2022. However, the agreement has still not been implemented.

The Margara checkpoint on the Armenian side has been ready for operation since December 2023. Despite the agreements reached, however, the border remains closed.

At the same time, there have been occasional signs of limited progress. Since 1 January 2026, for example, Armenia and Turkey have simplified the visa process for citizens of the two countries who hold diplomatic, special or service passports. Those staying in the neighbouring country for no more than 21 days can obtain an electronic visa (e-visa) free of charge.

Armenian-Turkish business forum in Yerevan

World.title: Armenia is building AI factory with Nvidia chips: what has been implemented for Azerbaijan under Washington agreement?
World.content:
What did the Washington agreement give Azerbaijan?

The US made Armenia’s access to advanced Nvidia processors one of the economic incentives offered during the peace talks. The project is already under way in Yerevan. Azerbaijan, meanwhile, received a strategic partnership document from Washington, the suspension of Section 907 and a number of pledges of cooperation. However, the road to Nakhchivan has yet to open.

Armenia will not manufacture Nvidia chips. But with a US export licence, the country is using them to build one of the region’s largest computing centres for artificial intelligence.

According to The Wall Street Journal, Washington used access to advanced Nvidia processors as one of the incentives intended to speed up a preliminary peace agreement between Armenia and Azerbaijan.

The Armenian government describes the project not as a reason for reaching the agreement, but as a “peace dividend” for the country. However, the launch of the Firebird project raises another question:

What concrete dividends has Azerbaijan received since the Washington agreement of 8 August 2025?

Armenia is already benefiting

The WSJ reports that US officials believed Nikol Pashinyan needed tangible economic gains from the peace process to offset the domestic political costs of an agreement with Azerbaijan.

As part of this effort, a US export licence for advanced Nvidia processors for the Firebird project in Armenia was included in the negotiations. The project was initially licensed to receive around 6,000 processors. Following the Washington agreement, the US authorised the export of another 41,000 Nvidia GB300 processors.

In August 2026, the first phase of the centre was launched near Hrazdan. According to the Armenian government, $500 million was invested in the first phase, more than 6,000 Nvidia Blackwell processors were installed and computing infrastructure with a capacity of 18 megawatts was built.

The investment is expected to exceed $4 billion in the next phases. By the end of 2027, the number of processors is expected to rise to more than 100,000, while infrastructure capacity is planned to exceed 400 megawatts.

The US did not provide Armenia with the chips free of charge. Investors are financing their purchase and the development of the infrastructure. The main advantage Washington provided was the export licence. Because access to the most powerful AI processors is subject to US national security controls, securing such a licence provides an economic advantage while also signalling political trust.

What did the US promise Azerbaijan?

On 8 August, Azerbaijan signed a memorandum with the US to establish a working group to prepare a Charter on Strategic Partnership.

The document outlined three areas of cooperation: regional connectivity, including energy, trade and transit; investment, including in artificial intelligence and digital infrastructure; and security cooperation, including defence supplies and counterterrorism.

However, the memorandum contained no legally binding commitments or funding guarantees. The two sides were expected to prepare a broader Charter on Strategic Partnership within six months.

The document was signed in February 2026 during US Vice-President JD Vance’s visit to Baku. The charter refers to the creation of AI data centres in Azerbaijan, defence supplies, energy projects, cybersecurity, demining and investment opportunities along the Middle Corridor.

Unlike the Armenian project, however, it does not name specific companies, investment amounts, the quantity of equipment or launch dates for the projects. Although the document says the two sides should agree on a list of projects and roadmaps for their implementation within three months, the full list has not been made public.

In June, the creation of a data centre in Azerbaijan was also discussed only as “potential cooperation” during a meeting between Azerbaijani Minister of Digital Development and Transport Rashad Nabiyev and a US delegation. The ministry’s statement did not name a specific investor, budget or construction schedule.

Section 907 suspended, but not repealed

One of the most concrete outcomes for Azerbaijan from the Washington meeting was the latest suspension of Section 907, which restricts direct US assistance to the country.

A decision by Donald Trump on 8 August 2025 temporarily removed restrictions on US security cooperation with Azerbaijan and the provision of US government assistance.

However, this does not mean that Section 907 has been repealed. It remains part of US law, while the president can only suspend its application. Ilham Aliyev has also said he expects Congress to repeal the provision completely.

During his visit to Baku, Vance also said the US would provide Azerbaijan with new boats to help protect its territorial waters. However, the statement did not specify their number, models, cost or delivery dates. There is also no publicly available evidence that the boats have so far been delivered to Azerbaijan.

Minsk Process closed: the main political gain for Baku

The most significant political outcome for Azerbaijan was the closure of the OSCE Minsk Process and related structures. This had long been one of Baku’s key demands.

The foreign ministers of Armenia and Azerbaijan signed a joint appeal on the issue in Washington. On 1 September 2025, the OSCE decided to close the Minsk Process, and the administrative procedures were completed on 30 November that year.

The previous international mediation mechanism for the Karabakh conflict was therefore formally abolished. The move has no direct economic impact, but it is important in terms of international recognition of the political reality that emerged after the war and was consolidated by Baku.

The road to Nakhchivan remains closed

One of the most widely discussed elements of the Washington agreement for Azerbaijan is the TRIPP project, which is intended to establish a connection between the country’s main territory and Nakhchivan.

However, the 8 August Joint Declaration does not give Azerbaijan an established right to transit. It only sets out the goal of creating “unimpeded connectivity” and says Armenia will work with the US to develop the framework for implementing the TRIPP project.

In January 2026, the Armenian government said that routes still had to be determined, a TRIPP company established, land-use issues resolved and construction permits issued. On 31 August, Aliyev and Pashinyan also discussed the “next practical steps” towards implementing the project.

Azerbaijan still has no operational road or rail link to Nakhchivan through Armenian territory. The route has not opened, transport operations have not begun, and the tariff and customs arrangements have yet to be tested in practice.

Two different “peace dividends”

It would be wrong to say that Azerbaijan received nothing from Washington. The application of Section 907 has been suspended, the Minsk Process has been closed, a strategic partnership with the US has been established, and new channels for defence and technology cooperation have been opened.

However, most of these outcomes are political in nature or remain commitments to future cooperation. Armenia’s benefit has already taken concrete and measurable form: an export licence has been granted, thousands of Nvidia processors have been installed and the first phase of a $500 million project has been launched.

Baku says it did not need economic incentives to reach an agreement with Washington. Hikmet Hajiyev, an aide to the Azerbaijani president, told the WSJ:

“We won the war and also wanted to achieve peace.”

This position may explain why the US offered a more concrete economic incentive to Yerevan. But the outcome remains the same: the Armenian part of the Washington package has already taken tangible form in a data centre, while a significant share of the commitments concerning Azerbaijan remains a promise for the future.

What did the Washington agreement give Azerbaijan?

World.title: Azerbaijan is building drone fleet on Caspian sea: what will SALVO and KAYRA change?
World.content:
Azerbaijan’s drone fleet in the Caspian

Azerbaijan has launched local production of armed naval drones and loitering maritime drones based on Turkish technology. The new systems are designed for a range of missions, from protecting energy infrastructure in the Caspian Sea and carrying out reconnaissance to attacking ships. However, the number of drones being produced, the cost of the programme and the share of manufacturing actually carried out in Azerbaijan have not been disclosed.

On 6 September, President Ilham Aliyev and First Vice-President Mehriban Aliyeva visited the Azerbaijani Navy.

The visit was intended to showcase two unmanned naval platforms: the SALVO armed uncrewed surface vessel and the KAYRA maritime kamikaze drone.

According to Azerbaijan’s presidential website, the drones are being produced by a joint venture between MİRAS, a defence industry company operating under Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Defence, and Turkish shipbuilder DEARSAN. Aliyev was briefed on the drones’ technical specifications before the systems underwent live demonstrations.

The official statement did not disclose production volumes, the cost of the project or when the first batch would be delivered to the Azerbaijani Navy.

They have been showcased before

SALVO and KAYRA are not being shown in Azerbaijan for the first time. SALVO was unveiled in August 2025 during military exercises focused on “the protection and defence of maritime energy infrastructure”.

KAYRA was presented in November that year at a military parade in Baku.

The significance of the 6 September presentation, therefore, is not the introduction of the systems themselves. The key change is that they are now being produced at a joint facility in Azerbaijan, and the production process was officially demonstrated to the country’s leadership for the first time.

This suggests that Azerbaijan wants to move beyond simply buying finished military equipment from Turkey towards domestic production, maintenance and potentially technology transfer. However, the official information does not make clear how much of the hulls, engines, electronics, communications and control systems is actually produced in Azerbaijan.

What is the difference between SALVO and KAYRA?

SALVO is a larger, multi-purpose platform designed for repeated use. KAYRA, by contrast, is a smaller kamikaze drone designed to rapidly approach and destroy its target.

Specification SALVO KAYRA Length 14.79 metres 7,6 metres Maximum speed More than 35 knots, around 65 km/h More than 60 knots, around 111 km/h Maximum range Up to 400 nautical miles, around 740 km 300 nautical miles, around 555 km Hull Aluminium Composite material Main role Patrolling, surveillance and armed operations One-way attack and target destruction

According to DEARSAN, SALVO can be used to patrol coastlines and borders, conduct reconnaissance, combat smuggling, carry out search-and-rescue operations and engage surface targets.

During tests conducted by the company in 2022, SALVO launched a Cirit missile made by Turkish defence company Roketsan, hitting a moving target. A stabilised 12.7mm machine-gun mount produced by ASELSAN was then tested. The platform can be controlled from a mobile station on shore, a command centre or another military vessel.

It is not known what weapons will be fitted to the SALVO platforms intended for Azerbaijan.

The missions listed for KAYRA are primarily offensive. According to its manufacturer, the drone is designed to strike enemy ships and patrol boats, naval bases, ports, coastal infrastructure and logistics routes.

The type and amount of explosive carried by KAYRA, its guidance system and its ability to operate autonomously if communications are lost have not been publicly disclosed.

Why are these systems needed in the Caspian?

One of the main tasks of the Azerbaijani Navy is to protect oil and gas infrastructure in the Caspian Sea, as well as ports, pipelines and the country’s maritime borders.

According to Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Defence, during naval exercises in 2025, ships patrolled and monitored areas where oil and gas pipelines run. They also practised responding to attacks by a simulated enemy, countering underwater sabotage groups and dealing with the threat of mines.

SALVO-type systems can carry out some of these tasks without putting ship crews at risk. They can conduct surveillance for extended periods, track suspicious vessels and, when armed, use force if necessary.

KAYRA, by contrast, is more of an offensive and deterrent weapon than a defensive one. Their small size and high speed could create additional challenges for the defences of warships. Using several such drones simultaneously from different directions could force a larger vessel to devote more resources to self-defence.

At the same time, drones do not replace a conventional navy. Their effectiveness depends on the quality of intelligence, the resilience of communications, operator training and their integration with other vessels into a unified command system. Electronic warfare, GPS jamming and loss of communications are considered key vulnerabilities of such systems.

Lessons from the war in Ukraine

The war in Ukraine has significantly changed perceptions of the role of naval drones in modern warfare. Ukraine, which does not have a large conventional navy, has used relatively cheap uncrewed boats to limit the capabilities of the Black Sea Fleet of Russia.

The experience has shown that smaller states can develop a maritime deterrent without having to build up large warships on a comparable scale. However, Russia has also strengthened its defences, port barriers and drone detection systems over time. This shows that the advantage provided by such technologies is not permanent.

The fact that Azerbaijan is producing KAYRA alongside SALVO, with KAYRA designed for one-way attacks, suggests that Baku is embracing this new model of naval warfare.

Will the military balance in the Caspian change?

The Caspian littoral states are Azerbaijan, Iran, Kazakhstan, Russia and Turkmenistan. The Convention on the Legal Status of the Caspian Sea, signed in 2018, calls on the parties to develop their military capabilities within “reasonable sufficiency”, maintain a balance of arms and ensure transparency. The convention also bans the presence of armed forces from non-littoral states in the Caspian.

Producing equipment in Azerbaijan based on technology from a Turkish company does not violate this ban. It involves technological and industrial cooperation rather than the deployment of foreign armed forces in the Caspian.

The emergence of two new platforms does not, by itself, alter the regional military balance. Assessing their impact would require knowing how many systems will be produced, what weapons they will carry and how they will be integrated with the rest of the navy.

There is also no public evidence that Azerbaijan is developing these systems specifically against Russia or Iran. Baku conducts joint exercises in the Caspian with Iran and Kazakhstan. Nevertheless, amid rapid rearmament and the spread of military technologies, neighbouring states are likely to take every new strike capability into account when planning their defences.

Key questions remain unanswered

The president’s visit officially confirmed that the naval drones are being produced in Azerbaijan. However, key information needed to assess the scale of the project remains undisclosed:

How many SALVO and KAYRA systems are planned for production?

How much will the contract and the production facility cost?

What share of the components will be manufactured in Azerbaijan?

What weapons and control systems will the Azerbaijani versions carry?

Have the systems already entered operational service, or are they still undergoing testing?

Who will decide when and under what procedures the kamikaze drones can be used?

SALVO could expand Azerbaijan’s surveillance and armed patrol capabilities in the Caspian, while KAYRA could provide a new asymmetric strike capability. Local production could also make maintenance easier and reduce dependence on foreign suppliers to some extent.

However, the actual capabilities of this “drone fleet” will depend on production volumes, how well the systems are integrated into a unified combat command network, and the financial terms of the project, which have not yet been disclosed.

Azerbaijan’s drone fleet in the Caspian

World.title: Azerbaijani activist living in France: ‘My father in Baku and I have received threats’
World.content:
Threats against Azerbaijani activist living abroad

Azerbaijani civic activist Ramazan Tagiyev, who lives in France, says he continues to receive threats over posts criticising the authorities on social media. He says the latest messages have also targeted his father, who lives in Baku.

“He said he knows where my father is in Baku”

Tagiyev says that on 3 September, a man named Rashad, who goes by the nickname “Roma”, contacted him again, threatening to beat and kill him. He also said he was currently in the French city of Toulouse and intended to track him down.

Tagiyev says that this time the threats also targeted his father, who lives in Baku:

“Rashad wrote that he knows where my father is in Baku and that he would make sure people found and beat him. The threat against my father is particularly worrying. It shows that the threats are no longer directed only at me but are now extending to my family.”

Threats began in March

The civic activist says the threats began in March 2026 after he started posting material on social media criticising the Azerbaijani government, state projects and prominent public figures.

At the time, he received calls from different unknown numbers as well as threatening messages.

Tagiyev says the situation escalated further in May after he published a critical post about Azerbaijani meykhana performer Rashad Dagly, who is currently serving a prison sentence for murder.

He says people living in Toulouse who, he claims, have links to criminal circles threatened to track him down and “deal with” him.

Fearing for his safety, Tagiyev left Toulouse soon afterwards.

Facebook account blocked after mass complaints

Tagiyev says that in August, following a series of posts about the Cavan TV project and bloggers, his Facebook page was hit by a wave of complaints, after which the account was blocked.

Tagiyev links the attacks on his social media accounts and the threats he received around the same time to his civic activism.

“What is Cavan TV and why did Tagiyev criticise it?”

Cavan TV is a media project run by the CAVAN Youth Movement, a public association targeting a young audience and receiving state support. Some of the movement’s projects receive financial and organisational support from the Youth Foundation of Azerbaijan and the Ministry of Youth and Sports.

Cavan TV is known for covering socially significant events using manipulative techniques. During high-profile events, such as the flooding of Baku after heavy rains, the platform has published material that shifts attention away from the responsibility of state institutions, eases public discontent and redirects the discussion towards secondary issues.

This was the focus of Ramazan Tagiyev’s criticism of Cavan TV.

Claims of links to criminal circles

Tagiyev says he learned about the past of the man who threatened him, Rashad, and his alleged links to criminal circles from Rashad himself.

The activist says Rashad told him that he had served two prison sentences in France and had links to criminal circles.

Tagiyev also claims that Rashad told him that some of the people accused of involvement in an attempted attack on Azerbaijani blogger Mohammed Mirzali, who lives in France, had stayed at his home.

According to the activist, Rashad also told him that he had come to Toulouse after an incident in Germany in which a man was stabbed, and threatened Tagiyev with “the same fate”.

Reported the threats to French police

Ramazan Tagiyev says he reported the threats to the French police. According to him, French law enforcement launched an investigation and located the man who had threatened him.

Jamnews was unable to independently verify Tagiyev’s claims with French law enforcement. The man named in the allegations has not been contacted for comment.

Threats against Azerbaijani activist living abroad

World.title: What do Abkhaz residents expect from Tbilisi? A video discussion with Abkhaz experts
World.content:
De-isolation of Abkhazia

Abkhaz journalist and editor of Chegemskaya Pravda, Inal Khashig, and civic activist Adgur Lagvilava discussed the key challenges facing Abkhazia’s foreign relations, as well as its ties with Georgia’s official authorities in Tbilisi.

Key points and arguments:

Fuel crisis and relations with Georgia: Resolving the gasoline shortage in part through purchases in Georgia sparked absurd accusations from the Georgian opposition regarding supplies to the Russian military.

Resolving the gasoline shortage in part through purchases in Georgia sparked absurd accusations from the Georgian opposition regarding supplies to the Russian military. Distorted perception of Abkhazia in Georgian society: A historically inaccurate narrative prevails in Georgia alleging that Abkhaz are an “alien people,” which is used to justify Georgian claims. Abkhazia has become a political simulacrum for Tbilisi, and ignoring Abkhaz agency hinders dialogue.

A historically inaccurate narrative prevails in Georgia alleging that Abkhaz are an “alien people,” which is used to justify Georgian claims. Abkhazia has become a political simulacrum for Tbilisi, and ignoring Abkhaz agency hinders dialogue. Politicization of history in Georgia: Georgian authorities pragmatically rewrite history and rehabilitate historical figures (such as King Heraclius II) to justify their current political course and rapprochement with Moscow. The speakers view this approach as a dangerous manipulation of the past for the sake of short-term gain.

Georgian authorities pragmatically rewrite history and rehabilitate historical figures (such as King Heraclius II) to justify their current political course and rapprochement with Moscow. The speakers view this approach as a dangerous manipulation of the past for the sake of short-term gain. Prospects for conflict resolution and Georgia’s European integration: To establish relations, Georgia must take responsibility for the 1992 war, officially recognize Abkhaz as an indigenous people, and repeal the “Law on Occupied Territories.” Promises of European integration are a “hollow sound” for Abkhazia, as the country is isolated from Europe and sits within the Russian information sphere.

To establish relations, Georgia must take responsibility for the 1992 war, officially recognize Abkhaz as an indigenous people, and repeal the “Law on Occupied Territories.” Promises of European integration are a “hollow sound” for Abkhazia, as the country is isolated from Europe and sits within the Russian information sphere. Abkhazia’s foreign policy: The Abkhaz authorities show passivity and miss international opportunities (for example, initiatives in the Turkish parliament), positioning the country as Russia’s “zone of responsibility.” The speakers call for actively developing an independent strategy of de-isolation to protect sovereignty and guarantee citizens’ rights.

Full text version of the conversation:

Inal Khashig: Hello! You are watching “Chegemskaya Pravda.” Another anniversary of the recognition of Abkhazia’s independence by Russia has passed. The festive events have once again brought to the forefront the issue of our development—the development of the Abkhaz state. And this topic resonates not only on its own, but also in the context of relations between Georgia, Abkhazia, and Russia, as well as the global situation. One way or another, there is much to think about. Today, our guest is Adgur Lagvilava. Adgur, good afternoon!

Adgur Lagvilava: Good afternoon, Inal.

Inal Khashig: Gasoline has finally reappeared, thank God.

Adgur Lagvilava: But it’s expensive.

Inal Khashig: But expensive, yes. Nevertheless, it is available, and thank God for that. Overall, the situation itself, of course, is far from pleasant. The fact that gasoline is back now does not mean that disruptions will not occur again. How do you view this entire situation when we have to, say, make up for the deficit from Georgia?

Adgur Lagvilava: Gasoline is not just a chocolate bar that you can easily forgo (though it’s probably better to give up chocolate). Gasoline is a strategic resource, the foundation of economic activity. Virtually all freight transport inside Abkhazia depends on fuel. Therefore, in the current situation, to provide the economy and the people with fuel, if we were able to take it from Georgia, I see no problem with that. We could also take it from other countries. We had similar experiences after the war: we bought fuel from Romania. Unfortunately, all these alternative supply routes ceased.

Right now, Russia is experiencing a complex fuel situation, and we ended up dragged into this crisis alongside them. If our fuel companies have the opportunity to get gasoline somewhere else to supply the population, I see no problem with it whatsoever.

At the same time, in Georgia itself, this was perceived very negatively—to the point where the opposition accuses the government, alleging that this fuel is supposedly being bought by the Russians for their military needs. That is entering the realm of clinical pathology.

Inal Khashig: For anyone who served in the Soviet Army, it is clear that little has changed in terms of weaponry systems. Most of the equipment—both Soviet and Russian—runs on diesel. In that light, such statements sound simply absurd.

On the other hand, one way or another, fuel enters Abkhazia from Russia, and it is insufficient for our market. But if the Russian military base were lacking gasoline, Russia would first and foremost take care of its own needs. At the very least, Rosneft, which is the primary supplier of gasoline to Abkhazia, would have supplied the Russian military bases first.

Therefore, such assertions are sheer nonsense. And when you read things like that from people who once held major state posts in Georgia—specifically, comments were made, it seems, by the former chairman of the National Bank of Georgia—it sounds extremely unseemly. I understand there is a domestic political agenda, but you cannot allow it to run on tracks where your statements will simply be laughed at.

Adgur Lagvilava: Incidentally, in this context, we have been observing Georgian discourse for many years. We receive precisely the information that is connected to us and occurs around us. One gets the impression that for Georgia’s internal political agenda, Abkhazia has become a sort of mythical country. It is recalled whenever some tension arises. Some use the topic of Abkhazia to direct negativity against the ruling authorities, while the ruling authorities constantly try to “reconcile” with us—though it is completely unclear on what basis all of this is supposed to happen.

That is to say, Abkhazia today is a simulacrum for Georgia that they created for themselves. The country they invented does not actually exist. Some say their territories are occupied; others claim that we in Abkhazia dream of returning to Georgia. They have their own sort of Abkhazia-Narnia, a Middle-earth of sorts in which they believe. Unfortunately, all these myths they constructed around Abkhazia have now maximumly obstructed our ability to obtain fuel. They bought into their own myths, and now it negatively impacts us because we do not know what tomorrow will bring. Perhaps Russia itself will temporarily run out of fuel, leaving us in a desperate situation. That is why our authorities must look for alternative avenues.

Inal Khashig: In any case, we won’t be left entirely without gasoline.

Adgur Lagvilava: I have serious doubts about that. If nothing is done about it…

Inal Khashig: Yes, but I think one way or another there will be gasoline. I am more concerned about the presence of a distorted understanding of the nature of the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict within Georgian society, government, and political circles. They hold a warped perception of the sentiment in Abkhazia. It seems to me that even the Abkhaz nation itself is perceived there in a distorted light: to them, we are some kind of “Apsuas” who descended from the mountains two or three centuries ago, while the real Abkhazia is allegedly something completely different.

What I am driving at is this: there are opportunistic approaches that clearly get in the way, but on the other hand, there are attempts by Georgia itself to change something, and this applies not only to Abkhazia. I have been observing the current discussions in Georgia surrounding the figure of the former King of Kartli-Kakheti, Erekle II, under whom the Treaty of Georgievsk was signed in 1783, placing Kartli and Kakheti under the protectorate of the Russian Empire. For many years after Georgia gained independence, Erekle II was considered a negative figure. Now, his rehabilitation is underway: last year, I believe, a monument to him was unveiled in Tbilisi, and now discussions surrounding his personality have intensified once more. Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze states that Erekle II effectively saved the Georgian people and their future, and that without the Treaty of Georgievsk, modern independent Georgia would not exist.

Reflections on what might have been are highly debatable, but the fact that Erekle II had very little choice at that moment is indisputable. Nevertheless, when history becomes a tool of political expediency, it is quite dangerous. I do not believe Erekle II wished harm upon his people. Historical facts speak volumes, even though the Treaty of Georgievsk did not save Tbilisi from Persian occupation a few years later. But things could have been significantly worse.

Currently, a segment of Georgian society views the rehabilitation of Erekle II quite negatively, perceiving it as a subtle indicator of a possible restoration of diplomatic relations between Tbilisi and Moscow and the conclusion of an alliance treaty. How do you view all of this? Saakashvili goes even further in his predictions, claiming there will be separate agreements with both Abkhazia and South Ossetia. What is your take on all these discussions, and what do you think about this matter?

Adgur Lagvilava: I am not deeply versed in Georgian history of the late 18th and early 19th centuries, but judging by our experience of living with Georgians in a single state, post-war events, and their historical discourse, Georgians frequently use history as an ideological foundation for the current political environment.

They have their own vision of who the Abkhaz are today. Perhaps it is not the official viewpoint, but a perception has taken root in Georgian society that we are an alien element who assimilated the local so-called “Abkhaz” by force of arms and began calling ourselves Abkhaz. This narrative has persisted from the very moment they developed claims over Abkhazia. Historical science and all kinds of pseudo-theories, such as Ingorokva’s famous concept, were tailored to fit this narrative.

If you look deeper into this process: since 2008, a narrative emerged (including in official documents) that we are a territory occupied by Russia. But that is merely the superficial layer. If the Georgians want to, they can peel it away simply by altering a few laws. At a fundamental level, however, they view us, the Abkhaz, as the occupiers. In their view, we occupied this territory after arriving 300–400 years ago from the North Caucasus and destroying or assimilating the Georgian population here.

When these historical narratives first emerged, they may not have carried direct aggression, but ultimately they led to the 1992 war. The radical segment of Georgian society gained an ideological and historical justification, which, naturally, bears a very distant relationship to genuine historical science. Authentic scholars—Georgian, Russian, and international alike—acknowledge this. Yet within Georgian society, this narrative remains potent, as is clearly visible across social media.

This issue could be resolved at the legislative level. Or the Georgian president or prime minister could simply step forward and state that the Abkhaz are an autochthonous people who have inhabited this land throughout their entire history, which aligns with reality.

Given how Georgians handle history, it seems to me that the current discourse surrounding the Treaty of Georgievsk also rests on political expediency—an ideological justification for the present rapprochement between Tbilisi and Moscow. I view it precisely within this context: in Georgia, history is used to justify the current political agenda or to steer it in the desired direction. I believe that is precisely the case.

Inal Khashig: As for the occupation: yes, according to their version, the Abkhaz once came down from the mountains and assimilated the local population. But regarding the occupation, they still maintain the view that Russia occupied the territory—and, by their logic, not in 2008…

Adgur Lagvilava: By their logic, we are an alien population here and ought to vacate this territory. Since we are an incoming element, we should leave Abkhazia.

Inal Khashig: Even if we were an alien people, how are we supposed to vacate the territory? How is that envisioned?

Adgur Lagvilava: In the manner they attempted in 1992.

Inal Khashig: For a state striving to join the civilized world and having declared a course toward Europe for many years, speculating about being “indigenous” or “non-indigenous” is a foolish endeavor altogether.

On the other hand, the thesis of “occupied territories” was originally launched by Saakashvili based on the events of 2008. But then their appetites grew, and now it turns out that Russia began the occupation as far back as 1992. Sometimes you watch broadcasts on the internet where participants ponder with a wise air that Russia started the war in 1992, as if the government and the State Council of Georgia had absolutely nothing to do with it.

Yes, there are many myths, but they lack a coherent picture. When you start asking questions from different angles, this logic collapses. Since the time of Eduard Shevardnadze, they have asserted that a certain “third force” prevented them from avoiding war. At the same time, they did not deny that they sent in troops. And who were those troops? The Mkhedrioni—criminals released from prisons. They explained that Abkhazia is Georgian territory. But if you send criminals who engage in looting and killing civilians onto your own territory against your own citizens, the state forfeits the moral right to that territory and those citizens.

At one time, Russian journalist Yulia Latynina formulated a statement drawing a bottom line under Georgia’s claims: Georgia lost the moral right to Abkhazia the first time when it sent in troops, and the second time when it lost that war. Frankly speaking, that is the starting point we must build upon.

When they appeal to a “third force,” it becomes a question of responsibility. If you are so easily manipulated that a “third force” can compel you to send criminals and cutthroats from the Mkhedrioni into territory you consider your own, what is your level of responsibility? How will you explain to the Abkhaz: “Sorry, the devil made us do it, it was all a third party”? Suppose we hypothetically resolved the conflict and found ourselves in a unified state. Where is the guarantee that some “third force” will not drive them mad again and lead them to wage war on us once more?

Referencing a “third force” demonstrates the failure of the state itself. How attractive must such a state be to the Abkhaz people, who endured the hell of war and lost 4% of their ethnicity, to spark a desire to unite with Georgia?

Another question: you cannot alter geography, and this conflict must be resolved in any case. Sooner or later, it will be resolved. To achieve this, one must talk to the Georgians—perhaps to win back something for their own citizens residing in the Gali district. Who knows what interests might exist. But all of this is resolved through negotiations. Yet how do you conduct negotiations if they believe their conflict is with Russia, not with us?

Adgur Lagvilava: For them, it is a very convenient position—to blame Russia for everything without delving into our actual relationship, problems, and historical context. After all, if Georgians truly immersed themselves in what transpired, they would have to recall more than just the 1992 war. There was the long Soviet period, the alteration of the status of the Abkhaz Republic within the USSR, assimilation processes, and resettlement.

If they objectively studied this history, they would have to draw certain conclusions and assume the main share of responsibility. But they do not want to do that, because then they would have to take concrete steps. It is far more convenient to blame Russia for everything—especially since the global context right now is such that “Russia is to blame for everything.”

If Georgian society and the state wish to take real steps toward us—we are not talking about recognition right now, which is a long-term prospect—the very first step must be the official dismantling of the narrative regarding the “alien” nature of the Abkhaz population. They could do this at least at the level of speeches by top state officials: officially declare that Abkhazia is the historical homeland of the Abkhaz and cease broadcasting these unpleasant assertions. Ideally, they could codify in their legislative acts that the Abkhaz are an autochthonous population. That would be a first step, and I do not believe acknowledging an objective historical truth is so painful for Georgian society. We are not demanding that they recognize us tomorrow and open an embassy here. One must begin precisely with this. And, of course, it is necessary to repeal the Law on Occupied Territories, which serves as the legal foundation of our international isolation.

Inal Khashig: Yes. You have probably read the transcript of the interview with Nika Gvaramia, one of the leaders of the Georgian opposition. He argues that it is necessary to stop picking at the past and reopening the wounds of Georgian society caused by the war and defeat, and instead move forward and speak about the future. As an opposition representative with a distinctly pro-European stance, he speaks about the European Union, the economy, and the need to showcase to the Abkhaz all the benefits the EU provides. How do you assess Georgia’s prospects in the context of the European Union, and how attractive is the European Union itself to Abkhaz?

Adgur Lagvilava: As far as Georgia is concerned, the agenda of European integration sounds much weaker there now than it did 10 years ago, when it was their primary foreign policy strategy. It seems to me that de facto Georgia is moving away from it.

Recall the events in Ukraine: Yanukovych also constantly spoke about European integration, even though he had no intention of executing it. But because a demand existed within society, he was forced to employ at least rhetorical tactics. I compare this to the current situation in Georgia: there is a young population oriented toward Europe, and the authorities cannot simply dismiss their political views, regardless of whether they favor joining the EU or rapprochement with Russia. Therefore, one should view this primarily from a rhetorical perspective.

If we look at the facts of recent years and read international reports on Georgia—European, American—the level of democratization, which is so crucial for the European community, is steadily declining in Georgia. A few years ago, I compared the metrics for Abkhazia and Georgia based on a report by World Vision (I might be mistaken about the organization’s name): our democratization metrics were higher than Georgia’s.

Furthermore, one must not forget that there are dozens, if not hundreds, of political prisoners in Georgia. Many opposition figures are under investigation, and criminal cases are opened over public statements. Georgia may rhetorically articulate plans to join the EU out of inertia, but de facto we see that the country is increasingly closing off.

The European agenda is fading further against the backdrop of cooling relations with the US. American leaders and the Deputy Secretary of State state this directly: a genuine chilling effect is observable. Many experts write that the White House’s focus has shifted further south—to Armenia and Azerbaijan—while Georgia remains on a residual basis. Against this backdrop, rapprochement between Tbilisi and Moscow is taking place. It appears that international support for Georgia today is much weaker than it was 10 years ago.

Inal Khashig: Yes, Georgian Dream lacks a clear goal to join the European Union for quite understandable reasons. After all, it is the party of Ivanishvili—an oligarch who accumulated his fortune quickly. For Europe, a person with such origins of capital looks questionable. On the other hand, without holding any official positions, he is the primary figure in the country, which cannot happen in Europe. With such a status, one is not admitted to the European Union.

However, that is the current situation, and what happens in the long term remains unknown. Georgian Dream is not permanent; sooner or later, the uninterrupted presence of a single political force in power becomes tiresome…

Adgur Lagvilava: Forgive me for interrupting. I do not claim absolute truth and do not consider myself a profound expert on Georgian political processes, but it seems to me that at a fundamental level, the Georgian people approve of Georgian Dream’s policies. Power is maintained not merely through heavy-handed measures. It appears to me that the majority of Georgians do not actually want movement toward Europe and the West, but rather support rapprochement with Russia. Georgian Dream possesses a strong electoral base. To me, this is a bit of a Georgian phenomenon.

Inal Khashig: On one hand, I wouldn’t put it quite like that. When for nearly 35 years—since the late 1980s—a pronounced anti-Russian card was played in Georgia and Russia was consistently portrayed as an enemy, such informational propaganda does not pass without leaving a trace. I see this in the scandals surrounding Russian tourists, where someone might be beaten, insulted, or refused service. On the other hand, a negative image is also forged by the existence of the Law on Occupation, when society is indoctrinated to believe that all problems, including the loss of Abkhazia and South Ossetia, arose because of Russia. Despite the fact that Georgia’s economy interacts closely with Russia’s, the negative image of Russia among the majority of the population persists, and this will be a defining factor for the future of Georgia itself.

Returning to Abkhaz realities: when Georgian politicians speak of attempting to “seduce” us with the European Union, one must understand that the EU has always been closed off to us. Under the Soviet Union, we did not know Europe, and then the war, blockade, and sanctions began. The Law on Occupied Territories prohibits any interaction with Europe, and Europe respects Georgian laws. Residents of Abkhazia are not issued visas, our passports are not recognized, and we have no trade or economic relations with the EU. We have grown accustomed to this; Europe is closed to us.

Adgur Lagvilava: We don’t even know what we are refusing.

Inal Khashig: Exactly. On the other hand, the majority of Abkhazia’s population resides within the Russian information space, where the narratives broadcast about Europe are far from positive. Why would the European Union be attractive to us?

For us to even consider whether we need Europe or not, it would be necessary to repeal the Law on Occupation, allow Abkhaz to travel freely around the world, and trade with European and other countries. Then, perhaps, our horizons would expand and our attitude toward the world would change. But this does not mean that Abkhaz would immediately decide to head toward the European Union. For the idea of European integration to have any prospect at all, they should first open the world to us, and then we will decide for ourselves. For now, while this world remains closed, the European Union is merely an empty phrase to us.

Adgur Lagvilava: It is an entirely dead agenda. It seems to me they formulate these points primarily for themselves, trying to find hypothetical paths to regain Abkhazia: “Let us show the Abkhaz the European Union!” Within Abkhaz society, this topic is not discussed at all.

Inal Khashig: In that same interview, Nika Gvaramia suggests not touching old wounds and speaking about the European Union. He is a politician and understands that describing Abkhazia and South Ossetia as a “lost cause” would mean putting an end to his career.

Nevertheless, a certain thought can be traced in his words: regaining the territories by military force will not succeed; there are no guarantees of victory in a new war. And if Georgia faces a choice—to move toward the European Union or to remain with dreams of restoring territorial integrity—his assertions nudge toward the idea of moving toward the EU, even if without formally relinquishing claims for now.

Europe is unlikely to want to assume responsibility for these unresolved conflicts. Therefore, a pragmatic understanding is emerging among a portion of the Georgian opposition: the perpetual desire to reclaim Abkhazia and South Ossetia hampers the development of Georgia itself. The seeds of this understanding already exist in society. Do you think such a scenario is possible?

Adgur Lagvilava: Regarding joining the European Union?

Inal Khashig: Regarding a pivot toward Europe, if sooner or later such a choice presents itself.

Adgur Lagvilava: It seems to me that in the coming decades, Georgia will not find itself in the European Union. Right now, the country has, one could say, pivoted toward Russia. This is clearly visible in economic relations: Georgia’s economic dependence on Russia today is significantly higher than on the EU.

All logistical projects being implemented in Georgia, even if targeted at Europe, have China and the US as their main beneficiaries. And talk about the EU is a narrative for internal consumption. There is a young segment of the population in Georgia that aspires to the West, travels extensively, and the authorities cannot simply wave away this agenda. They support it at the rhetorical level, but Georgia is taking no real steps toward joining the EU, nor will it in the near future.

The pragmatic element of the Georgian establishment and opposition understands that reclaiming Abkhazia through old Saakashvili-era methods will not succeed. Perhaps they calculate that Abkhazia will open up to Georgia not within a unified state, but on the foundation of some shared integration platform. The European Union in their vision is a structure more akin to the Soviet Union than a union of national states, where Abkhaz borders would open to Georgia. This is a pragmatic approach, but their overarching goal remains unchanged.

At the same time, today we are not prepared to join any integration platforms—neither the European Union nor any others—due to our economic, political, and military vulnerabilities. For us, this represents a colossal risk. We are extremely vulnerable economically: our entire recent political agenda and the resignation of the previous president were linked to economic risks. We are currently not ready for any integration.

If the Georgian authorities truly wish to make correct political moves, they must eliminate the primary landmine planted beneath our future relations—the narrative that we are an alien people. This is a fundamental issue about which the Georgian establishment remains silent. In Georgian society, the perception of us as alien occupiers has become dominant, and that is the bedrock for future conflicts. If they want to demonstrate a constructive approach, it is precisely this stereotype they must combat. The Law on Occupied Territories can be repealed in a single day, but changing society’s perception that Abkhaz are not an alien element is far more difficult. What basis can there be for good-neighborly relations if we are viewed as occupiers?

As for the European agenda, I would not take it seriously. But a major problem lies in how we ourselves behave. Georgians react to our silence: if we do not clearly state our path, where are we actually heading? They, for instance, want to join the European Union or align with Russia, but what is our foreign policy agenda? Our leadership speaks daily about internal issues and expresses gratitude to Russia, but performs no active work toward international recognition. We have found ourselves in the role of passive observers of the geopolitical processes occurring around us. We lack distinct foreign policy initiative.

In such a situation, Georgians interpret our behavior as a weakening of positions and a readiness to concede. A recent example: when a deputy from Turkey made a statement about the possibility of recognizing documents and establishing maritime and air communication with Abkhazia, our authorities effectively ignored it.

Inal Khashig: The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Abkhazia came out in support, but not a single pro-presidential or pro-government organization issued a statement.

Adgur Lagvilava: The Ministry of Foreign Affairs made a very vague statement in the spirit of “we favor all good things.” I would not attach great significance to it.

Inal Khashig: Nevertheless, it was stated there that they support it. But what bothers me most of all is that all these pro-government parties and various public organizations, which express their views on any occasion, remained silent in this context.

Adgur Lagvilava: Including the fact that neither the president nor the prime minister spoke out. Officially, only individual deputies stepped forward and expressed their support, whereas parliament itself as an institution did not speak out, even though this falls squarely within its domain. Through the Turkish parliament, it might have been possible to find some useful avenues. But the president remained silent, the prime minister remained silent, and pro-government organizations remained silent. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs issued a statement—and it is good that it did—but it was perceived more as a routine formality.

Inal Khashig: You see, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs did note the existence of the movement and welcomed it. But there is a nuance here: this agenda in Turkey itself is pushed by the opposition, by opposition organizations. I understand why the president or other state bodies might not have spoken out, but other public and political organizations could very well have done so. We have “Amtsakhara,” “Aytaira,” and “United Abkhazia,” which convene round tables every week. They ought to have spoken out!

I consider this a very important point. Remember the thesis pushed during the presidential elections about a certain “pro-Turkish” stance of the Abkhaz opposition or a segment of Abkhaz society? At that moment, all players in that field knew perfectly well that it was a suspicion entirely plucked out of thin air. But now it is working. It is entirely possible these pro-government organizations did not speak out precisely because they are afraid: what if someone dislikes it, what if it is seen as a movement toward Turkey, and so forth? This is a case where you spawn fake narratives and then fall victim to them yourself.

Adgur Lagvilava: That happens often—when you fall victim to your own propaganda.

Inal Khashig: Exactly, your own propaganda. It seems to me it is time to move away from this fake reality, from attempts to constantly portray a situation of perpetual celebration in Abkhazia. We must ensure that our economy develops and our sovereignty and security are strengthened. On this note, I will wrap up, but before doing so, I want to briefly return to your words…

Adgur Lagvilava: You mentioned that in Turkey, this process is being driven by opposition organizations. But after all, the locomotive of this process is the Abkhaz residing there. Sitting here in Abkhazia, I should not divide Turkish Abkhaz based on whether they belong to the opposition or support Erdoğan. Turkey is a large country with a great history; it has both a government and an opposition. Yet this initiative was supported by a third of the Turkish parliament—not five or ten individuals.

I voiced criticism regarding our reaction for this reason. Naturally, our society received this news with enthusiasm: genuine joy arose that at least some process of ending Abkhazia’s isolation had begun. But look at the situation from the outside. Step back from being an Abkhaz journalist and view everything through the eyes of an outside observer from another country who needs to examine what is happening in Abkhazia. In recent years, you do not hear Abkhazia declaring the need for international recognition. The impression is created as though we are already recognized by the whole world and belong to all international organizations, including the UN.

In fact, through our inaction, we position ourselves not as a state that strove for recognition, but as someone’s area of responsibility. Today, we are perceived as a territory within Russia’s sphere of responsibility, rather than an independent state pursuing international recognition and participation in international institutions. Any observer watches how a state reacts to ongoing processes. Our state ignored these events, and the Georgians read this perfectly well too. They see our reaction. I can imagine what a psychological blow the beginning of such processes in Turkey was for them. But then they see that our authorities do not react to it in any way. That is, through our own inaction, we demonstrate that we are prepared to shift our own positions.

That is what I was talking about. The point is not whether someone likes the Turkish position or whether there are hidden traps—nobody disputes that. But our state must react to such processes and demonstrate—even if it has no direct involvement in them—that this is part of our strategy.

Inal Khashig: I think it is important for the authorities in any case to formulate a strategy for ending Abkhazia’s isolation. And this applies to such moments as well. It is not strictly necessary to achieve recognition from yet another small Pacific island nation like Nauru, which might revoke its recognition a few years later. By and large, that is merely an emotional factor that has no bearing on our lives: we do not travel to Nauru, and we have no real contacts with them.

Adgur Lagvilava: Recognition of our passports by Turkey would be far more important than recognition by fifty islands in Oceania or the Caribbean.

Inal Khashig: Yes. That is one effective measure that could truly impact the lives of many of our citizens and numerous ethnic Abkhaz living in Turkey. The ability to travel around the world with Abkhaz passports is significantly more important—with all due respect to all the small states of the world with which, by and large, we have no contacts and are unlikely to have any in the near future, even if they recognize us. When we talk about ending isolation, the most important thing is our residents, our citizens, who will be able to move freely across the globe using Abkhaz documents. That is fundamentally important for us.

On this note, I will conclude our broadcast. Let us fight for the end of our isolation!

Adgur Lagvilava: For now, it seems to me, through our own efforts.

Inal Khashig: How else? Do you want someone else to fight for you?

Adgur Lagvilava: I mean—through the efforts of society itself.

Inal Khashig: That is precisely the point: it is always society itself that achieves these goals. Adgur, thank you very much!

Let me remind you that our guest today was Adgur Lagvilava. I bid you farewell. Goodbye, and until next time!
