The notice is due to the potential presence of blue plastic.

The supermarket said the cereal should not be eaten, but returned to stores for a full refund.

It said there have been no reports of injury or illness but anyone who had consumed the cereal and was concerned about their health should seek medical advice.

Woolworths said it took food safety seriously and apologised for the inconvenience.

World.title: One year on, we still don't know how Tom Phillips hid his children in the bush for four years
World.content:
One year on and it's still not known how Tom Phillips hid his children in the bush of Waikato's west coast for four years.

Phillips died following a shootout with police after they were called to reports of a burglary in the early hours of 8 September, 2025.

He had spent 1358 days in the bush with his children by that point and shot a police officer several times during the confrontation.

Child Matters CEO Megan West said the question on everyone's lips a year ago today was how this could have happened, and people were still waiting for answers.

In November, former attorney-general Judith Collins announced a public inquiry would look at whether all practicable steps were taken by government agencies to ensure the welfare and safety of Phillips' children.

It was received by the government in July, with the expectation it would be released in mid-August. A week later, the deadline was extended by a month "to clarify a matter".

"Without the answers to these questions, we cannot start putting the necessary safeguards in place to prevent a situation from getting to this point in the future," West said on Tuesday.

"While every situation involving children is unique, and this one even more so, many of the risks and warning signs are the same."

Police at the location of one of the campsites near Waitomo where Tom Phillips and his children had been hiding. Dean Purcell/New Zealand Herald via Getty Images

She said it needed to be asked at what points the child protection system, consisting of multiple agencies, failed in this case, and how the system could be improved.

"Those working at the frontline of child protection are constantly balancing risk, unknown factors, parental rights, and children's needs.

"This inquiry shouldn't be an attack on individual workers, rather a robust critique of a wider multi-agency system that isn't providing the right training, funding, or support to enable sound decision-making."

West said the Phillips case reinforced that children could be known to the system, but not safe.

"More needs to be done to enable agencies to work collaboratively and close the gaps that are allowing children to fall through the cracks.

"Despite being known to the system, ultimately the Phillips children's needs became invisible to health, education, justice, and child protection agencies, the error only being realised once it was too late."

She said releasing inquiry findings was the crucial step needed to identify specific failings and start building a safer, more robust network around vulnerable children, including immediate and extended family, community, and government.

"Without this, more children will become invisible to the system that is meant to help them."

West said the Phillips case wasn't alone in highlighting the need for systemic change, referring to a review into the killing of baby Mustafa Ali by his father Mukzameel Ali.

An Oranga Tamariki office, whose handling of the baby's death was the subject of the scathing internal review, also managed the Tom Phillips case.

"The internal baby Mustafa review identified several failings, including minimal analysis of risk, insufficient monitoring, and a lack of basic knowledge of practice and legislation among some workers. Again, multiple agencies were involved and questions remain on how this case unfolded.

"This is undeniable proof that we need an integrated, information-sharing system that goes beyond words on paper and genuinely implements legislative and child-centric frameworks."

World.title: Woman and two children killed in Rotorua home
World.content:
A man has appeared in court charged with assaulting a person in a family relationship after a woman and two children were killed in Rotorua.

Police earlier said they arrived at a property on High Street in Glenholme shortly before 10.30pm on Monday, where they found two dead children and a woman with life-threatening injuries. The woman died at the scene.

Police said a man was assisting police with their inquiries.

* Do you know more? Email sam.sherwood@rnz.co.nz

Police at the scene this morning. NZME

On Tuesday, a man aged in his early 20s appeared in the Rotorua District Court charged with assaulting a person in a family relationship.

The court heard that court documents named three victims. The man, who appeared via audio-visual link, was wearing white coveralls.

The man, and the victims, were granted interim name suppression.

The man was remanded in custody until 2 October.

A relative of the man declined to comment when approached by RNZ.

Google Maps

Earlier, Bay of Plenty acting district commander Inspector Logan Marsh said it was an "incredibly traumatic incident for all those involved".

"Our focus now is on supporting the family, our first responders and getting answers to what occurred last night," Marsh said.

"We know this event will be felt widely in the community and people will want answers. We are methodically working through the scene, including a detailed forensic examination."

He said this could take several days and there would be a police presence in the area.

"We know people will be understandably shaken following this incident and police will be carrying out additional reassurance patrols over the coming days and nights in Glenholme and the wider community.

"Out of respect for the victims and their family, we ask that people refrain from speculation or conjecture. Our focus remains on establishing exactly what occurred and providing answers for those affected."

World.title: New Zealand troops to continue to train Ukrainian soldiers
World.content:
The government has renewed the deployment of New Zealand troops training the Ukrainian Army.

Up to 70 Defence Force personnel will be deployed in Europe until June 2028 as part of Operation Tīeke.

The majority will be training Ukrainian soldiers in Poland as part of a multinational initiative, led by Norway.

Defence Minister Paul Goldsmith said Ukrainians deserved New Zealand's support for their courage and fortitude.

"The NZDF's support through operation Tīeke will prioritise training in specialist areas such as electronic warfare and drone operations, capabilities that are critical to Ukraine's self-defence," he said.

New Zealand will also continue providing intelligence, liaison and logistics support in Europe.

Foreign Minister Winston Peters said New Zealand continued its condemnation of Russia's aggression, and its support of Ukrainians.

"The defence of Ukraine has significant implications not only for the security of Europe, but also for the Indo-Pacific," he said.

World.title: NRL finals: Warriors-Dolphins qualifying final at Mount Smart sells out within minutes
World.content:
It took just minutes for Warriors fans to fill Mount Smart Stadium - at least on paper.

Tickets for Saturday's NRL qualifying final against the Dolphins sold out almost immediately after going on sale to the general public at midday on Tuesday, ensuring the Warriors will run out in front of a packed house of around 25,000.

Warriors members had already snapped up their allocation after sales opened yesterday, while Dolphins members got access from 6pm.

General public sales opened at midday on Tuesday and within minutes, the remaining tickets were gone - much to the disappointment of fans.

Shortly after tickets went on sale, upset Warriors fans took to social media to vent their frustration at missing out.

"I missed out on all three sale times, and I'm a member! Not impressed," wrote one fan on the Up the WAHS facebook group.

"So shit, been trying since yesterday," wrote another.

It is unclear whether the Warriors will make any additional seating available.

The sell-out crowd sets the scene for a boisterous reception for the Warriors as they begin their NRL finals campaign at home.

The Warriors have put themselves in a strong position to contend for a maiden NRL premiership, with their second place finish at the end of the regular season guaranteeing themselves two home play-offs, starting on Saturday against the third-placed Dolphins.

If they lose to the Dolphins their next game will be the following week in the semi-finals. If they win, the Warriors will earn themselve a week off and the right to host a preliminary final.

The demand for tickets for Saturday's match will likely put further pressure on Warriors' officials to move their final home play-off game to the Eden Park, which, with a capacity of 50,000, can hold roughly double the number of fans as Mount Smart.

The finals series is controlled by the NRL, which according to its policy "reserves the right, at its sole discretion to determine venues considered most suitable to host the NRL and NRLW final series matches".

Warriors chief executive Cameron George said he was happy the NRL agreed to play their opening play-off game at Mount Smart, but confirmed Eden Park remains on the table for the second game.

"That was really important to me that I challenge NRL's thinking on taking it away because it's our home, it's where we've got fans that sit there in the rain, hail or sunshine for many, many years and it's so connected to us and our players love it there, our fans love it there and we've earned the right to play it there," George said.

George said a decision on where that second game will be played is unlikely to be made until after the Warriors play the Dolphins.

"My promise to [NRL boss] Peter V'Landys was that after we get through this weekend, we see where we're at and then we can discuss what it looks like moving forward. But just happy it's at home this weekend."

"At the end of the day, the NRL own the finals. So the reality is they can tell us where to go and play it and when to play it."

V'landys told the Sydney Morning Herald that the expected groundswell of support for the Warriors meant a move to Eden Park was virtually inevitable for the club's second play-off game.

"I'd say you'd be 90 per cent sure that we'll be going to Eden Park," V'landys said.

"We've discussed it with the club. They'd like to stay at Mount Smart, but they realise that if all goes to plan, they're going to have a massive audience and they'll be accommodated at Eden Park."

World.title: Fishing company, tech entrepreneur give large donations to NZ First
World.content:
New Zealand First has banked major donations from a kina fishing company and a tech entrepreneur, latest filings reveal.

RNZ is tracking the money flowing to the parties this election year and where it is coming from.

In an update on Tuesday 8 September it was revealed tech entrepreneur Brian Cartmell donated $100,000 to NZ First on the same day he donated the same amount to ACT, which was previously reported. Cartmell also gave to Opportunity earlier in the year, and donated to National in 2025.



NZ First also received $30,000 from Cando Fishing, a company that markets itself as “the premium provider of top-quality Kina” from the South Island. It had not previously donated more than $20,000 to any political party, according to Electoral Commission records.

Labour’s donation total has also been boosted by new, large donors. The Electoral Commission record shows five regular donors of smaller amounts to the party now tipping over the $20,000 mark. When donations go over this amount, they must be promptly disclosed to the commission.

Labour’s donors include a company called Coromandel No 5 Ltd, tech entrepreneur Martin Buhr, Ross Galloway, Paul Grimshaw and David Wills. The combined total of these newly reported donations to Labour was $111,975.

To date, coalition parties have received 73 percent of declared donations.

Here’s where things stand across all parties for declared donations of over $20,000.

When the donations made to the parties in the governing coalition are combined, the spread looks as below.

Who are this election's big donors?

The following donors have given $100,000 or more so far in 2026.

Not all donors are individuals. Companies, trusts and unions also give to political parties. The chart below shows the split between organisational and individual giving over $20,000 for each party.

In the 2023 election, unions gave $335,000 to Labour. National received no donations from unions, but did receive more than $1m from businesses.

Exploring the data in the below chart shows where donors have focused on a single party or donated to more than one party.

Each line represents a donor with wider lines indicating larger amounts.

How the money grew

Donations of $20,000 and more made from the start of the year are captured on the below chart.

If someone makes numerous donations under $20,000, once the cumulative total tops $20,000 it must be declared.

How much bigger could the donation pot grow?

The below chart shows the 2023 annual total of donations over $20,000, compared to the current 2026 total.

Some who donated in 2023 haven't given more than $20,000 so far in 2026 to the same party. The table below identifies who these donors are.

Each row represents a party. A donor may appear more than once if they gave to multiple parties in 2023.

The following donors haven't donated before 2026.

How we analysed the data

All original data comes from the Electoral Commission website. RNZ's analysis normalises names which may appear more than once, but with different treatment. For example a John Smith and J Smith with the same address are updated to both be John Smith. In some instances where people have given individually as well as jointly their names are collated. If Joan Smith had the same address as John Smith and had donated individually, as well as made a joint donation with John Smith, the name is updated to John and / or Joan Smith.

Donation dates are taken from the "date received by party" information. In some cases one donation entry will consist of several donations made over time. The date received is the date on the donation return and should be the date the total donated by the donor tipped over $20,000.

World.title: Mixed emotions as Andreeva embraces injured idol after US Open win
World.content:
US Open fans have witnessed a display of sportsmanship as Mirra Andreeva tended to and consoled an injured Anastasia Potapova as the fifth seed won their fourth-round match.

Potapova jarred her knee as she lost the first point of what turned out to be their final game on Louis Armstrong Stadium, prompting Andreeva to rush to the other end of the court to check on her.

She helped the 24th seed up and Potapova was able to limp to her bench, where Andreeva asked if someone could bring her ice.

The French Open champion finished off the next three points for a 5-7, 6-4, 6-3 victory that sent her to the quarterfinals in Flushing Meadows for the first time, jogging around the net again for a warm embrace.

"It's not the perfect end to the match," 19-year-old Andreeva said.

Potapova appeared to be tearing up as Andreeva came around the net for a long embrace after the final point.

Potapova represents Austria but was born in Russia and still played under that flag when she won the junior Wimbledon championship in 2016.

"For me, Nastya, she was always like a prodigy," Andreeva said of her 25-year-old opponent.

"She came on tour early. She also had a lot of wins. I also remember we were all watching and cheering for her when she won juniors Wimbledon title. I remember watching that match.

"For me, she was always, like, a little star that I was kind of always looking at."

Potapova (right) appeared to be tearing up as the pair embraced after match point. (Getty Images: Pete Staples/USTA)

Potapova won their first meeting on tour in 2022 but Andreeva has won the past four, preventing Potapova from reaching her first grand slam quarterfinal.

"First, she just beat me. So after, I just kind of knew that she's a tough player to play, but at the same time, she was so nice," Andreeva said.

"Then since then we would practice together, and just like that, the more you see each other, the more you spend time together, then you just talk about everything, discuss everything. Then, just like that, I feel like we have a good connection off the court."

Elsewhere, Qinwen Zheng mounted another extraordinary fightback to upset six-time major winner Iga Świątek and reach the quarterfinals.

Qinwen Zheng is the first qualifier since 2021 to make it this far in the women's draw. (Getty Images: Al Bello)

Zheng has become Flushing ‌Meadows' most entertaining escape artist this year, coming back from a 0-5 deficit in the deciding set against third-round foe Madison Keys.

She let the first five games slip through her fingers in 20 minutes against 2022 champion Świątek before digging in, and she collapsed to the court with her hands ⁠in her face after sealing the win on the fourth match ‌point.

China's Olympic champion is the first qualifier ​since Emma Raducanu in 2021 ‌to reach the quarterfinals of the women's draw, as she battles back from a chronic elbow injury that had stunted her career.

Two-time winner Naomi Osaka was summarily swept aside by second seed Elena Rybakina, who won 6-1, 6-4 in just over an hour.

Coco Gauff, the 2023 champion, beat 18-year-old Iva Jovic 6-1, 6-4 in an ​all-American clash to decide the final women's quarterfinalist.

Gauff will face Andreeva, and Rybakina will take on Zheng. On the other side of the draw, third seed Jessica Pegula faces Emma Navarro, while world number one Aryna Sabalenka is up against Wimbledon champions Linda Noskova.

World.title: Everything you need to know ahead of NFL Melbourne
World.content:
American Football will roll into the MCG for a regular-season NFL match for the first time on Friday.

The San Francisco 49ers will take on the Los Angeles Rams, who are the nominal home team for the game.

This will be the first regular-season NFL game ever hosted in Australia, although American Football matches have taken place in the country before.

Here's everything you need to know about the game.

When is the game?

Davante Adams (left) will look to continue his excellent form into the new year. (Getty Images: Brooke Sutton)

The game takes place on Friday morning AEST, with kick-off at 10:35am.

That is what time kick-off will be in Victoria, New South Wales, Queensland, Tasmania and the ACT.

In the Northern Territory and South Australia, that is a 10:05am kick-off. In Western Australia, kick-off will be 8:35am.

This is to cater for the Thursday night television audience in the United States, with a New York kick-off time of 8:35pm, while in LA the game will get underway at 5:35pm.

If you are going to the game, the gates open at 7am local time, with access to the Yarra Park precinct, which the NFL has dubbed the NFL Stadium Campus.

There will be food, entertainment, sponsor activations and fan activities to keep punters busy once they get inside.

Who is playing?

The 49ers and the Rams will meet in their season opener. (Getty Images: Brooke Sutton)

The Los Angeles Rams and San Francisco 49ers are the two teams who are set to play in this historic clash.

The Rams are the home team and come into the season as one of the favourites for this year's Super Bowl, with a stacked offence and miserly defence.

If you think the Rams sound familiar but the LA bit is confusing you, that's because the team has moved around a bit.

The team was formed in 1936 as the Cleveland Rams, moved to LA in 1946, but then shifted to St Louis in 1995, where they stayed for 20 years.

In 2015, the Rams moved back to Los Angeles.

You don't need a hat like this, but I'm sure it will help. (Getty Images: MediaNews Group/Pasadena Star-News/Keith Birmingham)

They are two-time Super Bowl Champions, winning their most recent in 2021. They play at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood.

The 49ers have always expected to reach the play-offs at an absolute minimum and will think they can do so again, despite a season beset by injuries last year.

Formed in 1944, the 49ers have always been based in the Bay area, although they currently play outside San Francisco at Levi's Stadium in Santa Clara.

They have won five Super Bowls, but have not won one since 1994, despite appearing in three Super Bowls since then, most recently in 2023.

How can I watch?

The game will be available to watch in Australia on Fox Sports/Kayo or on free-to-air on Channel Seven or 7Plus.

Coverage starts from 10am AEST.

Are tickets still available?

Want to join the Rams fans? There's still time. (Getty Images: Icon Sportswire/Greg Fiore)

If you'd rather watch the game live, as of Monday, there are still tickets available, both standing and seated, for the game at the MCG.

You can purchase the tickets via Ticketmaster.

Why is the NFL playing in Australia?

Heading into the 2026 season, there have been 62 regular-season NFL games played away from the USA.

Starting in 2005 with Mexico City, the NFL has gradually expanded its global reach, with games in nine different cities so far, with two more added in 2026.

Melbourne, Paris and Rio de Janeiro join London, Mexico City, Toronto, Berlin, Frankfurt, Munich, São Paulo and Madrid in hosting regular-season matches.

The idea is to spread the gospel and increase the global presence of a league that has no international competition outside of America.

MCG joins illustrious list

The MCG adds itself to an exclusive list of stadiums. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Morgan Hancock)

Here's a pub quiz stat for you — the MCG will become the fifth stadium to host an NFL game and the opening/closing ceremony of an Olympic Games.

The Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum (1932, 1984), Berlin's Olympiastadion (1936), London's Wembley (1940) and the Estádio do Maracanã in Rio de Janeiro (2016) have all hosted an Olympic Games opening ceremony, as did the MCG in 1956.

The Stade de France (closing ceremony at Paris 2024) will join it on that list when it hosts its first game later in the season.

Given the Rams are the home team, they will now have hosted matches at two different Olympic stadiums, having played at the Coliseum between 1946-1979 and 2016-2019.

Perhaps less surprisingly, the MCG is the first stadium to have hosted a Cricket World Cup final and an NFL regular-season game, so there is that.

At 100,022, the stadium has the largest capacity of any that will be used by the league this season.

Players to watch: Rams

Matthew Stafford had a career-best year in 2025. (Getty Images: Kevin Sabitus)

Quarterback Matt Stafford led the league with 4,707 passing yards and 46 passing touchdowns last season, with just eight interceptions.

That was one reason why the Rams' offence was the best in the entire league, averaging 30.5 points per game last season.

He has two elite wide receivers in his armory in Davante Adams and Puka Nacua, who was rated as the fourth-best player in the entire league by the NFL cohort.

The potential issue is that Stafford is now 38 years old and has historically struggled to back up productive passing seasons in the past.

Defensively, Myles Garrett was recently polled as the number one player in the NFL by his peers, and it's easy to see why.

According to the NFL players, Myles Garrett is the best player around. (Getty Images: Ric Tapia)

The 30-year-old defensive end led the league in sacks (23) and tackles for loss (33) last season for the Browns and his acquisition fills a gaping hole that was ruthlessly exposed as the Rams struggled down the stretch in 2025.

It's not just Garrett who has come in, though. The Rams have recruited two elite cornerbacks in Trent McDuffie and Jaylen Watson.

They will also welcome back Super Bowl-winning defensive tackle Aaron Donald, who has come out of retirement to lead the defensive line one last time.

Players to watch: 49ers

Two of the 49ers best players either side of the ball; defensive end Nick Bosa and tight end George Kittle, are coming off serious injuries from last season, so all eyes will be on how they front up when they suit back up this year.

Brock Purdy will want to iron out his interceptions this season. (Getty Images: Luke Hales)

On the defensive side, the 49ers pass rush is a genuine concern, especially if Bosa can't return from the ACL injury that ended his season, which means former Dallas Cowboy Osa Odighizuwa may need to really up his game from defensive tackle

Offensively, Brock Purdy will be desperate to stay fit for long enough to really get into a rhythm this season.

Last year the young quarterback started just nine games and managed a TD/INT ratio of 20/10. That's too many interceptions for an elite quarterback and, given the addition of quality wide receivers Mike Evans and rookie De'Zhaun Stribling, the Niners fans will hope he can find his accuracy.

Given all those new toys for Purdy to play with, running back Christian McCaffrey shouldn't need to be thrown to as many times as he was last year.

Christian McCaffrey got through a mountain of work in 2025. (Getty Images: Ezra Shaw)

The running back had an astonishing 102 receptions — the sixth most of any player in the league — for 924 yards and seven touchdowns last season.

That's in addition to his day job of running with the ball, where he had 1,202 yards from 311 rushes for 10 touchdowns, the eighth most rushing yards of anyone in the league.

His backup is likely to be Kaelon Black, so keep an eye on him as to whether he can carry some of that running load this season.

World.title: Cricket Australia green lights BBL privatisation, defying power states
World.content:
The Big Bash League will be partially privatised, in what looms as one of the most significant shake-ups of Australian cricket in decades.

Cricket Australia will defy heavyweight states New South Wales and Queensland to forge ahead with plans to allow states to explore sell-offs of 49 per cent stakes in their BBL franchises.

The decision to proceed was effectively made at a Cricket Australia board meeting last week, and will be officially green lit on Monday night.

BBL privatisation 'inevitable': CA Cricket Australia chief executive Todd Greenberg says private investment in the Big Bash League is "inevitable" and waiting for too long could mean "we've missed the boat" as more competitions pop up around the world.

It is understood a formal announcement will be made by Cricket Australia on Tuesday, in concert with several superstars of Australian cricket — a coup, given some initial pushback from the Australian Cricketers' Association.

However, there remains several details to be ironed out between the ACA and the CA, which has argued, amongst other things, for a greater share of revenue for its players.

The ACA insists it's supportive of privatisation as long as the long-term interests of the game are protected.

The players' union will continue to negotiate with Cricket Australia over, among other things, just how big a slice of the pie the players will receive.

This will form part of a new memorandum of understanding between the two parties.

Tasmania, Victoria and Western Australia are in support of the decision, that will allow states to undertake a market sounding process for the sale of 49 per cent stakes in their teams.

BBL privatisation became more of a reality when Cricket Victoria made plans to sell the Melbourne Renegades franchise earlier this year. (AAP Image: James Ross)

But power states New South Wales and Queensland remain opposed to the plan and will undoubtedly be rankled by Cricket Australia's decision to press ahead without them fully on board.

South Australia remains lukewarm on the concept but is more open to the idea than New South Wales or Queensland.

New South Wales has long believed an injection of private equity would largely amount to a sugar hit, and broader structural reform is needed to ensure Cricket Australia's financial viability into the future.

Cricket New South Wales has been contacted for comment.

Cricket Australia believes the privatisation will allow the BBL to keep up with other domestic T20 competitions around the world, such as India's IPL. (AP)

In contrast, Cricket Australia believe that privatisation of the BBL will allow the league to keep pace with rival competitions around the world, with proceeds to be spread throughout the broader Australian cricket ecosystem.

Transactions could be complete before the start of next season.

It is likely that prospective international team owners will be courted across the upcoming summer, with potential buyers expected to be in Australia to cast their eye over this year's BBL tournament.

In June, the privatisation process was accelerated when Cricket Victoria pre-emptively made plans to sell the Melbourne Renegades, while retaining the Melbourne Stars licence.

Several state CEOs recently travelled to India and the UK to connect with prospective buyers, ahead of being given formal approval to commence a sell-off process by Cricket Australia.

World.title: V'landys accuses NRL players of 'not telling truth' on rule confusion
World.content:
Peter V'landys has accused players of "not telling the truth" about set-restart confusion, as a survey of finals captains revealed ongoing uncertainty around the ruck.

The topic of set restarts is set to dominate the NRL finals, after Melbourne star Harry Grant claimed widespread frustration from players at the weekend.

The Melbourne captain declared most no longer knew what constituted a fast or slow play-the-ball, and the NRL needed to decide between being rugby league or touch football.

An AAP survey of captains and representatives at Monday's finals launch backed up Grant's claims, with six of the sides indicating they were still not entirely clear on what ruck speed referees wanted.

According to V'landys, Storm skipper Harry Grant (pictured) has 'got it wrong' when it comes to set-restarts. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne )

Also raised by players was the fact there is no chance to ask for clarification, given the game rolls on quickly with a set restart.

But V'landys disagreed, pointing to the fact there are only two reasons for set restarts and players had become more compliant for offside ones.

"I don't buy that," ARL Commission chairman V'landys said.

"The wrestling's got to go. The fans did not like the wrestling, they didn't like people slowing down the ruck speed. And we've accommodated that.

"The players know when they're trying to control the ruck speed.

" I think that they're not telling the truth if they believe when they're giving a six again, they didn't know what it was for. I mean, I think it's pretty obvious. "

Set restarts increased dramatically over the first half of the season, before dropping off through the State of Origin period and rising again in recent weeks.

The rise at the start of the year coincided with the NRL expanding the area in which they can be awarded to from 60 metres of the field to 80.

V'landys indicated they would not be repealed next season, rejecting Grant's claims there was confusion this year.

"I have the ultimate respect for Harry, and Harry's an absolute ornament of the game, but he's got this one wrong," V'landys said.

"When you look at the facts, the ruck speed is still the same as it was last year. It's around 3.5 seconds, and it remains that way.

Sharks co-captain Cameron McInnes (pictured) backed up Grant's viewpoint over the players' confusion. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

"Some teams try to take advantage of the ruck and slow the ruck down … we make no apology that we're going to keep the ruck speed the same for both teams.

"The raw numbers don't back up what Harry is saying."

The majority of club representatives surveyed on Monday did not blame referees, but suggested there was still some grey area around ruck interpretation.

"With some of the six agains, who knows what they are for," Cronulla co-captain Cameron McInnes said.

"I just think about a fan watching at home … you just see them and think 'what was that for? It was like the tackle before'.

"That's a problem."

Warriors captain Roger Tuivasa-Sheck (pictured) is concerned that a faster game will lead to more injuries for the players. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

Asked if he shared the same confusion, McInnes suggested he did.

"I get the clear as day ones where guys are taking the piss … but then there are flops and re-grips that don't get called as well," he said.

"I don't know what their mindset is, but there will be some at the start of the game that is given a six again, and others that are not."

Some players at the NRL finals launch also raised concerns around whether a faster game had prompted an increased injury toll.

"I feel like it's not a clear understanding [of the interpretation]," injured Warriors veteran Roger Tuivasa-Sheck said.

"As players we understand they want a faster and more entertaining game, but they're risking that with the number of injuries every team has.

"That's what they have to weigh up.

"Yes we're building a very entertaining game and people love the product. But at the same time you lose all these big players out."

AAP

World.title: Knee scans reveal heartbreaking verdict for luckless Swans captain
World.content:
Callum Mills has suffered more September heartbreak, with scans confirming the Sydney captain has torn his anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) in his right knee.

The defender could also potentially miss the entire 2027 season after he went down with a serious knee injury during Sydney's 53-point upset of the Brisbane Lions.

Mills's knee gave way as he attempted to corral Brisbane's Will Ashcroft near the boundary, late in the first quarter after an understrength Swans outfit burst to a 40-8 lead.

Swans coach Dean Cox was already expecting the worst in the aftermath, with scans on Monday confirming the injury.

Mills will meet with a specialist to determine a date for surgery.

It is the latest setback for the luckless 29-year-old, who missed the Swans' 2024 grand final loss with a hamstring strain he picked up before the preliminary final.

Mills had played just seven games in 2024 after hurting a shoulder in a "Mad Monday" wrestling contest with a teammate.

This year was the first time the defender had played more than 20 games since Sydney's 2022 grand final run.

The upset victory against Brisbane followed a tumultuous few weeks in the fallout from the Pullman Hotel scandal.

Mills was seen on crutches as his Swans teammates celebrated their win over the Lions on Saturday. (Getty Images: Matt King)

Mills has earned significant praise for leading the Swans through the turmoil, which past players have admitted shattered the club's famed "Bloods culture''.

Star players Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner and Nick Blakey — All-Australian contenders before they were banned from being selected — are among the five serving club-imposed bans.

Important tagger James Jordon and defender Riley Bice are the other Swans who won't play again this season.

Cox's selection conundrum is further complicated with key forward Joel Amartey (Achilles) and winger Justin McInerney (hamstring) nearing full fitness.

Hayden McLean — playing as cover for Amartey — slotted three majors against the Lions, with fellow talls Charlie Curnow (five goals) and Logan McDonald (six) also busy.

AAP

World.title: AFL acts to reduce head trauma at training for men and women
World.content:
The AFL will introduce limits on contact training for the 2027 men's and women's season in a bid to reduce concussion and head trauma.

All 18 clubs will be required to audit contact training and provide training vision to the AFL on request as part of regulations announced on Monday.

The measures dictate limits for the upcoming men's pre-season, with in-season training and an AFLW framework to be later introduced.

Set by week, measures start from a total limit of 120 minutes, which includes 60 minutes of high-intensity contact training.

AFL hits Geelong with monster fine over concussion waiver scandal The AFL hands down its penalty after a meeting between the commission and Geelong regarding Jake Kolodjashnij's now-controversial contract.

From week five of pre-season, the standard limit will be a total of 160 minutes and 120 minutes of high-intensity training.

Clubs will not be allowed to put players through high-intensity contact training on consecutive days, with teams recommended to use these high-intensity drills sparingly across all contact levels.

Consulting across disciplines from coaches to club doctors and data analysts, the contact training limits follow the 2023 recommendations from the Victorian coroner's investigation into the death of former Richmond player Shane Tuck.

Tuck died by suicide in July 2020 and was subsequently diagnosed with the degenerative brain condition chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE).

A separate consultation process will commence in September to develop similar limits with adjustments for the AFLW.

Shane Tuck died in 2020 and was subsequently diagnosed with CTE. (AAP: Mal Fairclough)

These measures are not mandated for community football, with the league preparing the next release of its local football concussion guidelines.

Concussion and head trauma is one of the most pressing issues facing the AFL.

The training framework comes after the AFL last month fined Geelong $140,000 over Jake Kolodjashnij's concussion waiver.

In 2024, Geelong struck a secret agreement with Kolodjashnij whereby he took on legal responsibility for future brain trauma in a bid to exonerate the club and its medical staff from court action in the future.

Multiple players, including former Melbourne star Angus Brayshaw, champion West Coast defender Jeremy McGovern and premiership Magpie Nathan Murphy, were forced into retirement due to repeated concussions.

There is also a multi-million-dollar concussion class action case against the AFL, led by former Geelong defender Max Rooke, in the Supreme Court of Victoria that is set to go to trial next year.

AAP

World.title: 'Not value for money': Plans for Tuggeranong ice sports facility scrapped
World.content:
The ACT government has announced a proposed ice sports facility intended for Tuggeranong will not go ahead.

Plans for the facility featured two international-standard ice sheets for figure skating, ice hockey, broom-ball and speed skating.

But the government said today that despite extensive discussions with advocates of the project, it has been unable to reach an agreement on a way forward at the Tuggeranong site.

Sports Minister Chris Steel said an evaluation of an updated proposal to build and manage the facility found the project "did not represent value for money for the territory".

Canberra Brave players have been calling for an upgraded training facility. (ABC News, Monte Bovill)

Updated proposal presented 'unacceptable risks'

The multi-purpose ice sports facility, dubbed Canberra Arena, was promised by ACT Labor during its 2016 election campaign, and at one stage of the project's planning, the completion date was even listed as 2025.

In addition to the government investment of $16.265 million, the remaining funds needed to build the estimated arena — estimated at $70 million at one stage — were to come from developers Cruachan Investments and Pelligra Holdings, who would "build, own, operate and maintain it".

"Unfortunately, we haven't been able to find a way forward with the partners Cruachan and Pelligra to build, maintain and operate this facility in Tuggeranong," Mr Steel said.

"The tender evaluation found that unfortunately there were a range of unacceptable risks and the updated proposal that was provided to the ACT government in January did not represent value for money for the ACT government."

Chris Steel says he's disappointed the project will not progress. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

Mr Steel said the proponents "were asking for more than double the territory's contribution to the project" in their latest updated proposal.

"That was one of the factors that led to the proposal being deemed not to be value for money," he said.

Cruachan chief executive Stephen Campbell said he supported the government's decision as additional costs associated with developing the site had become "prohibitive".

"We look forward to presenting a new proposal to the government in the coming months that will be more cost-effective, better meet community needs, and create improved access opportunities for all Canberrans," he said.

He said the Tuggeranong site was "too challenging" and the new proposal would include options for different locations.

Money to be spent on other sports facilities

Mr Steel said the $16.265 million that was committed to the facility would instead be spent "dollar for dollar" on upgrades to other sporting infrastructure projects in Tuggeranong.

Sporting clubs in the ACT have been invited to share their sporting and recreation infrastructure needs via a survey, which will inform how the money is spent.

"This investment will not be lost for Tuggeranong. The investment will go back into Tuggeranong to improve sporting infrastructure," he said.

Debate about the future site of a dedicated ice sports facility continues. (ABC News, Monte Bovill)

The proposed dedicated arena was to be a new training and competition facility for a variety of ice sports teams who currently use the aging Philip Swimming and Ice Skating Centre.

At one stage it was also to be a new home for the Canberra Brave ice hockey team which has been using a temporary ice rink set up at the Australian Institute of Sport in recent years.

Mr Steel acknowledged that the outcome would be "deeply disappointing" for the ice sports community.

"Now we will need to continue to work with our ice sports community on what the next steps are and what other opportunities there are to improve ice sport facilities in the ACT," he said.

"It's important to note that on the current Phillip site, the requirement for an ice skating facility that meets national competition standards still remains."

'Not the end game'

ACT Ice Sport Federation spokesperson Sandi Logan said they were "profoundly disappointed" but that it was "not unexpected".

"We've not had a great deal of confidence in recent times in the proponents' ideas and the proposals that they put up to amend the original concept of a community facility for the ACT ice sports community," he said.

"The second thing I'd say is that we've moved into overtime, this is not the end of the game.

"There's still a lot of work ahead of us, and we're grateful that Sports Minister Chris Steel and the ACT government continues to support us.

"And we're in a way grateful that we'll have another chance to come up with a better arrangement, a better partnership, and a better opportunity for the community to pursue ice sports in Canberra and the ACT."

The Phillip Swimming and Ice Skating Centre is now being run by Geocon. (ABC News: Joel Wilson)

He praised Geocon for how they had been managing the Phillip ice skating facility since taking over as lessees at the site.

"And maybe, just maybe, Geocon is looking at the Philip ice rink with a possibility for something into the future. I have no idea," he said.

"But we know that they have backed the Philip ice rink, maintained it, in fact, improved it to a state where we can now go with regular certainty that there'll be ice, there'll be a game, there'll be a sport to play."

Mr Logan said the foundation was in it "for the long run" until a solution was found.

"The ice may be thin under us, we may be skating on the proverbial thin ice, but we're here for the long haul, and we need to get a new ice rink built for the community."

World.title: Swans AFLW star says club's men's and women's players closer than ever
World.content:
Believing Sydney's men's and women's teams are closer than before, AFLW star Cynthia Hamilton has described the embattled club's resilience amid turmoil as "actually beautiful".

Hamilton is urging fans to continue their support, vowing the Swans won't disappoint on the field in Sunday's Sydney derby against rivals GWS at Henson Park.

The Swans women play in the Harbour City for the first time since the SCG double-header in round two, having played a home game in Coffs Harbour in round three.

Swans offer timely reminder of what 'Bloods' culture is meant to look like Many questions were asked about Sydney's famed culture in the wake of the Pullman Hotel scandal. As the finals got underway, the players showed exactly what it is supposed to look like on the field.

Fans came out in force at the SCG in the immediate aftermath of the men's Pullman Hotel scandal, with a crowd of 16,672 turning up for the victory over Essendon.

The attendance more than doubled Sydney's previous highest crowd for a home AFLW game.

In contrast, the men's team recorded its lowest SCG crowd of the season, just 30,058 fans watched them beat North Melbourne.

Star players Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner and Nick Blakey — All-Australian contenders before they were banned from being selected — are among the five serving club-imposed bans.

Important tagger James Jordon and defender Riley Bice are the other Swans who won't play again this season.

Errol Gulden (right) has been getting Sydney's men's and women's players together for breathwork sessions. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

As the men's team aims to rebuild respect for the famed "Bloods" culture, Hamilton says the club have come together even over the smallest of details.

"This has honestly brought us closer. We're doing breathwork in the morning together, we're doing little things," Hamilton said.

"Errol Gulden's been flicking the message [about breathwork] across to join both teams together as an opportunity to come closer.

"The boys have been bloody awesome. They've really brought the two groups together.

" In light of what's happened, it's actually kind of beautiful how the club has reacted. I would say we're closer than what we were before. "

As a healthy contingent followed the women's to Whitten Oval last week, the men's team enjoyed renewed support for their 53-point qualifying final upset of reigning premiers Brisbane and played in front of 37,261 fans at the SCG.

"When you look on the weekend, and you see the support the boys are getting, and then vice versa when we were at the SCG as well, it just shows how special the Bloods bond is and that the culture is there," Hamilton said.

"Keep getting around us, keep showing up, and we won't disappoint, hopefully."

GWS forward Tarni Evans also threw her weight behind the Swans, after urging fans to support the AFLW fixture at the SCG last month.

Sydney's AFLW side has received a mountain of support from both inside and outside the club. (Getty Images: Kelly Defina)

The 14th-placed Giants are looking to retain derby bragging rights and bounce back from a dour 31-point away loss to the Lions, taking a three-game losing streak to Henson Park.

Sydney is also licking its wounds after a 27-point defeat to the Western Bulldogs, leaving the Swans fifth after a first loss of the season.

Both sides have claimed two wins from four previous derbies in the women's league.

"This weekend, this is such a great opportunity in women's sport, to get out and support it," Evans said.

"Getting people to the game is unreal and that's what we want.

"This weekend will be another testament to that, a great game of footy to watch."

AAP

Tech.title: First Xiaomi, then the world: why Arm might give phone gaming a huge graphics boost
Tech.content:
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

China is getting first crack at a British technology that might change how mobile games are made and played. Today, the Xiaomi 18 Fold launches in mainland China with an Arm Mali G2-Ultra NX graphics processor inside its custom Xring O3 chip. What’s so special about that? After five years of development, Arm now has an AI gaming graphics accelerator inside its GPU.

By following Nvidia’s playbook, Arm-powered phones are about to have PC-like technologies to make games run faster, at higher resolution, with advanced lighting techniques, all without using more power than they do today. The jagged edges you see in the mobile versions of popular games might begin to go away.

And these advancements won’t just be locked to Chinese phones. The chips, devices, and games are already inbound.

“You will be able to buy it; you will be able to get it in phones next year, you will be able to get it in other types of larger screen devices, whether that be tablets or Chromebooks,” Arm’s Chris Bergey, EVP of Edge AI, tells The Verge in an interview.

While he can’t say which other devices will contain the Mali G2-Ultra NX, he hints that some of Google’s upcoming Googlebooks might use this graphics tech as well.

“We think it’s going to be huge,” Bergey tells me.

DLSS for Android

There are two ways to look at Arm’s new Arm Mali G2-Ultra NX. One is that it’s stronger than prior mobile GPUs, period, with an alleged 85-percent performance increase over the GPU that Xiaomi was using previously, and a 14 percent increase over Arm’s previous flagship in “non-AI gaming.”

But the other, more important way is that it enables a suite of hardware-accelerated graphical techniques that sound very similar to Nvidia’s DLSS, including AI upscaling (where it imagines a higher-resolution image), frame generation (where it generates new “fake” frames between existing ones), and even ray reconstruction like Nvidia’s DLSS 4.5.

“This really is about bringing Tensor-like capabilities into the GPU shader,” Bergey tells us. Image: Arm

Arm is calling all of these techniques “neural graphics,” but it doesn’t mean quite the same thing as when Nvidia uses that term — we’re not talking about enhancing faces by reimagining how light and shadow work, at least not just yet.

Note: Games won’t necessarily feel four times faster even if they look that way. Image: Arm

Instead, these improvements are about speed, offering what Arm claims is up to four times the framerate when “Neural Super Sampling,” “Neural Frame Rate Upscaling” and “Neural Denoising” are all applied simultaneously, because each technique lets the system do less work rendering actual pixels and frames, counting on AI to fill in the rest.

Note that games likely won’t feel four times faster, though, even if they look that way. Half of the boost is because your phone will imagine new frames between existing ones — and when Nvidia, AMD, and Intel do “frame generation,” it typically comes with the cost of additional latency.

Regardless, these techniques won’t all arrive immediately. “The first titles will largely be super sampling,” says Bergey, with frame gen coming in early 2027 and denoising “soon after that.”

But when you put them together, he says a phone can now genuinely play an experience like this Neural Dawn technology demo, below — and without draining your battery fast. “It might be like, hey, you can now play 1080p, 60 frames per second for three hours,” Bergey tells me. “In the past, it was 30 minutes.”

With the Xiaomi Pad 9 Pro Max tablet, which pairs Arm’s GPU with a larger battery, screen, and surface area for cooling, may offer even more performance. The Chinese company is showing off 3.2K resolution at 120 frames per second.

Bergey says that an entire phone with these chips will consume no more than 2.5 watts, with only 1.5 watts allotted to the GPU. “That’s basically what you want for real sustained gaming where it’s not getting warm in your phone, you’re not like ‘Oh, where’s my charger,’ that kind of thing,” says Bergey.

Or, he says, device and chipset makers can run this GPU at lower wattage to last longer. It’s not just for gaming phones: “This is not overclocking, this is mainstream,” he says. “This is about AI replacing traditional rendering; anywhere you can use it, you will use it,” he says.

Xiaomi claims its flagship Xiaomi Pad 9 Pro Max tablet, with the same Xring O3 chip, can play games at 3.2K resolution and 120fps. Image: Xiaomi

It’s not just for premium phones and tablets, either: “While Mali G2-Ultra NX targets flagship smartphones, neural graphics will also be available across the Premium and Pro configurations, bringing the technology to a broader range of mobile segments and tiers.”

Arm isn’t the only one attempting to push these speed-boosting PC technologies into the mobile realm. The developers of the graphically intensive Stellar Blade, for example, recently revealed they’re making their game run at 60fps on the Nintendo Switch 2 by using both Nvidia’s DLSS and a version of AMD’s frame generation technique. The Switch 2 has an Arm-based mobile chip too, though it contains a custom Nvidia GPU.

Like with the most advanced versions of Nvidia, AMD, and Intel’s techniques, game developers will need to integrate Arm’s features into their games, though participating game engines like Unreal Engine and Unity can help. Bergey doesn’t think it’s a switch gamers will be able to flip for just any game they like.

Arm’s partners. Image: Arm

Where Winds Meet, Infinity Nikki and Arena Breakout: Infinite are the first three games confirmed to take advantage of Arm’s new graphics accelerator, and Bergey tells us more games are on the way. Some will be announced in the coming weeks, he says — he’s just not allowed to reveal them quite yet.

Tech.title: Audi’s new A2 E-tron is its most affordable and efficient EV yet
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

When shopping for an electric vehicle, affordability is becoming a more common trait. But affordable and energy efficient is truly a rare breed. Often you have to sacrifice one for the other. Want something affordable? Great, here’s a range loser. Want something that goes the distance? Be ready to pay the price.

Surprisingly, here comes Audi to split the difference. The German automaker’s new A2 E-tron compact crossover is inexpensive, starting at just £32,200 (about $45,000). And it absolutely impresses with an ultra low drag coefficient and a range of battery and drivetrain options that, when configured correctly, can produce a range of up to 401 miles.

Unfortunately for us Yanks, this rear-wheel drive compact car is just for the European market for now. But perhaps Audi will eventually see the error of its ways, or Americans will get their heads out of their tailpipes long enough to see the real advantages of a highly efficient, compact EV with an Audi badge.

Previous Next









1 / 6

Efficient is often synonymous with aerodynamic, and the A2 E-tron certainly confirms that. Flush door handles, cool air intakes, a fully enclosed underbody, and gap reducers around the wheel arches help reduce the drag coefficient down to 0.24, a first for Audi. Another first is bidirectional charging, which will help support vehicle-t0-load via an outlet in the trunk, or vehicle-to-home with the right compatible DC wall box.

With the right motor and battery setup, the A2 E-tron consumes just 12.8 kWh per 62 miles (100 km), while the real mile-eater of the lineup manages up to 401 miles (645 km) on the European WLTP cycle. Inside, the A2 E-tron features a standard curved MMI panoramic display that combines an 11.9 inch digital gauge cluster with a 12.8 inch center touch screen.

Previous Next











1 / 7

There’s also plenty of clever storage thanks to a Fidlock magnetic fastening system that allows owners to click things like cupholders and charging cable bags into dedicated points around the cabin and trunk. Cyclists may be familiar with the tech that can keep their water bottles attached to their bike without a cage, but Audi says this is the first time it’s making an appearance in a production car.

While Audi gave up on its EVs-or-bust pledge last year, the automaker is leaving the door open for a mix of gas, hybrid, and electrification. The A2 may not be appearing alongside its brethren like the impressive S6 Sportback E-tron at the dealership anytime soon, but nothing is set in stone.
